docs.title: Section 3.4: Simulation and Verification: The Digital Sandbox
docs.text:
If you’ve ever spent forty-eight hours straight in a dark lab, staring at an oscilloscope and wondering why your FPGA isn't working, you’ve learned a painful lesson: Hardware is a terrible place to debug. On hardware, everything is invisible. You can't see the internal signals, you can't stop time, and every change takes thirty minutes to compile.

In the AMD UltraFast Methodology, we live by a simple rule: If it hasn't been simulated, it doesn't work. Simulation is your "Digital Sandbox." It’s a controlled, virtual environment where you can see every single wire, pause the clock, and inject errors at will. Finding a bug in simulation takes minutes. Finding that same bug in hardware can take weeks.

docs.title: The Simulation Mindset: Finding the Needle
docs.text:
Verification isn't just about seeing if your code "works." It’s about trying to break it. You should be your own harshest critic. If your testbench only tests the "Happy Path" (where everything goes right), you haven't really verified anything. You need to test the "Sad Path"—the overflows, the resets, the illegal states, and the random delays.

Think of simulation as a flight simulator. You don't want the pilot’s first experience with an engine failure to be at 30,000 feet. You want them to have experienced it a hundred times in the simulator first. Your FPGA logic is the same. Put it through the ringer in the digital sandbox so it’s ready for the real world.

Brain Power If your simulation passes but your hardware fails, what are the top three things you should check? (Hint: Think about timing, asynchronous signals, and power-up sequences.)

docs.title: Anatomy of a Testbench: The Virtual Lab
docs.text:
A testbench is a piece of HDL code that surrounds your design (the DUT or Design Under Test) and provides it with inputs. A good testbench has three distinct parts:

  1. The Stimulus: The part that generates the input signals (clocks, resets, data packets).
  2. The DUT: Your actual design, sitting in the middle of the lab.
  3. The Checker: The part that watches the DUT’s outputs and compares them to the expected results.

Too many engineers stop at step 1 and 2. They generate some inputs, look at the waveforms, and say, "Yeah, that looks about right." This is dangerous. Waveform staring is not verification. You need an automated checker that tells you—in plain English—if the test passed or failed.

docs.title: Fireside Chat: The Waveform Starer and the Verification Engineer
docs.text:
Waveform Starer: "I've been looking at these green lines for three hours. The data seems to be shifting correctly, and the enable signal is toggling. I think we’re good to go."

Verification Engineer: "Did you check if the packet header is correct? Did you verify the checksum on the output? What happens if the FIFO overflows mid-transaction?"

Waveform Starer: "Well... I didn't see any overflows in the ten microseconds I simulated. And I can't really read the hex values in the checksum very well."

Verification Engineer: "Exactly. That’s why I wrote a self-checking testbench. It ran 10,000 random transactions in the background while I was at lunch. It caught three corner-case failures that you never would have seen on a waveform. My testbench is the judge; the waveforms are just the evidence."

docs.title: Self-Checking Success: The Power of Assertions
docs.text:
A self-checking testbench uses Assertions to monitor the design. An assertion is a statement like: "If 'valid' is high, 'data' must not be zero." If that statement is ever false, the simulation stops and screams at you.

SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) are a powerful way to codify your design’s requirements. Instead of trying to imagine every possible failure, you just define the "Rules of the Road." If the design breaks a rule, the testbench catches it instantly. It turns verification from a subjective art into an objective science.

docs.title: The Coverage Map: How Much is Enough?
docs.text:
"How do I know when I'm done testing?" This is the million-dollar question. The answer is Code Coverage. Modern simulators can tell you exactly which lines of your code were executed and which weren't.

If your coverage report shows that your "Error Handling" logic was never triggered, you haven't tested your error handling! You need to go back and write more stimulus to hit those "uncovered" areas. Aim for 100% statement and branch coverage for any critical block. If you haven't seen it run in simulation, you can't trust it in hardware.

docs.title: Gate-Level Reality: The Final Audit
docs.text:
Most of the time, we simulate at the RTL level (the raw code). It’s fast and easy to debug. But RTL simulation doesn't account for real-world timing delays or the physical layout of the chip. That’s where Gate-Level Simulation (GLS) comes in.

GLS is slow—it can be 100x slower than RTL simulation. But it’s the only way to catch "gate-level" issues like timing violations on asynchronous paths or errors in the synthesis process itself. You don't need to run GLS for your whole design, but for critical interfaces (like a custom DDR4 controller), it’s the final audit before you release your product.

docs.title: Code Detective: The Clock Race Condition
docs.text:
A common mistake in testbenches is creating a "race condition" between the clock and the data.

// Code Detective: Why is this data capture unreliable?
initial begin
    data = 8'hAA;
    #10 clk = 1;
    #10 clk = 0;
    data = 8'hBB;
    #10 clk = 1;
end
// Hint: When exactly does the 'clk' rise relative to the 'data' change?

The flaw here is that the clock and the data are changing at the exact same simulation time step (#10). In a simulator, this can lead to "non-deterministic" behavior. Depending on the simulator's internal event queue, the DUT might see the "old" data or the "new" data.

Be precise about why, because the standard actually defines this. Both the clock edge and the data change land in the same time slot's active region, and the ordering of two blocking assignments across different processes in the active region is explicitly unspecified. Your DUT's always_ff and your testbench's stimulus are racing, and which wins is a property of the simulator, not of your design.

The fix — three techniques, in increasing order of robustness:

// 1. Drive stimulus from non-blocking assignments. NBAs are scheduled in the
//    NBA region, which is strictly after the active region, so the DUT samples
//    the OLD value at the edge - exactly like real hardware.
initial begin
    data <= 8'hAA;
    @(posedge clk) data <= 8'hBB;
    @(posedge clk) data <= 8'hCC;
end

// 2. Better: drive from a clocking block, which makes the skews explicit and
//    removes the question entirely.
clocking cb @(posedge clk);
    default input #1step output #2ns;   // sample just before, drive 2 ns after
    output data;
    input  result;
endclocking

initial begin
    ##1 cb.data <= 8'hAA;               // '##' advances by clocking-block cycles
    ##1 cb.data <= 8'hBB;
end

// 3. Best for anything non-trivial: generate the clock in one place, with a
//    period parameter, and never write a bare '#' delay in stimulus again.
localparam time TCLK = 10ns;
initial begin
    clk = 1'b0;
    forever #(TCLK/2) clk = ~clk;
end

The rule that prevents the whole class of bug: stimulus is driven <= after the edge; checks are sampled just before the edge. A clocking block states both in one place, which is why every serious verification methodology uses one.

docs.title: Analogy → Silicon
docs.text: In the story In the silicon / the testbench Where the analogy breaks Flight simulator RTL simulation of the DUT with generated stimulus A flight simulator models known physics; an RTL simulation models your description, so it cannot find a bug that exists equally in your RTL and your expectations The judge, not the evidence A scoreboard: a reference model plus an automated comparison Judges weigh grey areas; a scoreboard is binary, which is its value — it removes the human who wants the test to pass Rules of the road SystemVerilog Assertions (assert property) checking temporal behaviour Road rules are enforced when observed; an assertion fires only if the stimulus reaches the situation, which is why coverage and assertions are a pair The coverage map Code coverage (statement, branch, toggle, FSM) and functional coverage (covergroup) A map shows territory you know exists; code coverage cannot show you a feature you never implemented, which is what functional coverage is for The final audit Gate-level simulation with SDF back-annotation An audit re-checks the same books; GLS checks different things — synthesis correctness, X-propagation at reset, asynchronous path behaviour Testing the "sad path" Error injection, backpressure, reset during transaction, protocol violations Sad paths sound exceptional; in a real system they are the normal case under load, and they are where most field bugs live

docs.title: Do the Math
docs.text: "How much simulation is enough?" has a numeric answer more often than people expect.

docs.title: Coverage closure: how much stimulus does a goal imply?
docs.text:
Suppose you must cover every combination of a 4-bit opcode and 3 pipeline states, and your stimulus generator picks both uniformly at random.

\[\text{Bins} = 2^4 \times 3 = 48\]

Random sampling until every bin is hit is the coupon collector's problem, whose expected number of draws is:

\[E[n] = N \times H_N = N \times \sum_{k=1}^{N} \frac{1}{k} \approx N(\ln N + \gamma)\]

With \(N = 48\) and \(\gamma \approx 0.5772\):

\[E[n] \approx 48 \times (\ln 48 + 0.5772) = 48 \times (3.871 + 0.577) = 48 \times 4.448 \approx 214\]

About 214 random transactions to hit all 48 bins on average — not 48. And that is the mean; the tail is long, so a 99 % confidence target needs roughly two to three times more. Two consequences:

  • Constrained-random with coverage feedback beats pure random by a large factor. Once you are down to the last few bins, targeted stimulus finds them in tens of transactions where random needs hundreds.
  • If your bin count is \(2^{32}\), no amount of random simulation will close it. That is the signal to switch to formal property checking for that block, or to redefine the coverage model around meaningful equivalence classes rather than raw values.

docs.title: Simulation throughput: what your test plan actually costs
docs.text:
Givens — measure your own; these are typical orders of magnitude:

Quantity Value RTL simulation speed 5,000 DUT cycles per wall-clock second Gate-level with SDF 50 cycles per wall-clock second Design clock 400 MHz Scenario to verify 10 ms of real time \[\text{Cycles} = 10\times10^{-3}\ \text{s} \times 400\times10^{6}\ \text{Hz} = 4\times10^{6}\ \text{cycles}\] \[T_{\text{RTL}} = \frac{4\times10^{6}}{5000} = 800\ \text{s} \approx 13\ \text{minutes}\] \[T_{\text{GLS}} = \frac{4\times10^{6}}{50} = 80{,}000\ \text{s} \approx 22\ \text{hours}\]

Verdict: the 22-hour number is why "just run GLS on everything" is not a plan. GLS is for targeted questions — reset X-propagation, a specific asynchronous interface, the synthesis of one critical block — not for regression. And the 13-minute number tells you something useful too: a regression of 50 such scenarios is an overnight job, which means your nightly regression is a real thing you can have, and your per-commit smoke test needs to be a much smaller subset.

docs.title: The Real Artifact
docs.text:
A self-checking testbench with the four parts that matter: a clocking block (no races), a reference model, a scoreboard, and assertions. This is the skeleton to copy.

// tb_fifo.sv - self-checking testbench for a synchronous FIFO.
//
// The four properties that separate this from waveform-staring:
//   1. A clocking block, so stimulus and sampling cannot race the DUT.
//   2. A reference model (a SystemVerilog queue) that is obviously correct.
//   3. A scoreboard that compares every output beat and FAILS THE TEST itself.
//   4. Assertions for the protocol rules that a scoreboard cannot see.
//
// Run: xsim / xvlog -sv tb_fifo.sv fifo.sv ; then check the exit status, not the log.

`timescale 1ns/1ps

module tb_fifo;

    localparam int DW    = 32;
    localparam int DEPTH = 16;
    localparam time TCLK = 4ns;          // 250 MHz

    logic          clk = 1'b0, rst_n = 1'b0;
    logic          wr_en, rd_en;
    logic [DW-1:0] wr_data, rd_data;
    logic          full, empty;

    always #(TCLK/2) clk = ~clk;

    fifo #(.DW(DW), .DEPTH(DEPTH)) dut (.*);

    //--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 1. Clocking block - drives 2 ns after the edge, samples 1step before it.
    //--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    clocking cb @(posedge clk);
        default input #1step output #2ns;
        output wr_en, wr_data, rd_en;
        input  rd_data, full, empty;
    endclocking

    //--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 2 + 3. Reference model and scoreboard.
    //    The model is a queue. It is trivially correct, which is the point:
    //    a reference model complex enough to have its own bugs is not a reference.
    //--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    logic [DW-1:0] model [$];
    int unsigned   beats_checked = 0;
    int unsigned   errors        = 0;

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (rst_n) begin
            if (wr_en && !full) model.push_back(wr_data);

            if (rd_en && !empty) begin
                automatic logic [DW-1:0] expected = model.pop_front();
                beats_checked++;
                if (rd_data !== expected) begin
                    errors++;
                    $error("beat %0d: got 0x%08x expected 0x%08x",
                           beats_checked, rd_data, expected);
                end
            end
        end
    end

    //--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 4. Assertions - the rules a scoreboard structurally cannot check, because
    //    they are about signals rather than about data.
    //--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // Never write to a full FIFO.
    assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
        !(wr_en && full))
        else $error("write while full");

    // Never read from an empty FIFO.
    assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
        !(rd_en && empty))
        else $error("read while empty");

    // full and empty are mutually exclusive for a non-zero-depth FIFO.
    assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
        !(full && empty))
        else $error("full and empty asserted together");

    // After a write to an empty FIFO, empty must deassert on the next cycle.
    assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
        (empty && wr_en) |=> !empty)
        else $error("empty did not clear after write");

    //--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 5. Functional coverage - what did we actually exercise?
    //--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    covergroup cg_fifo @(posedge clk);
        cp_occupancy : coverpoint model.size() {
            bins empty_c    = {0};
            bins low        = {[1:3]};
            bins mid        = {[4:DEPTH-4]};
            bins nearly_full= {[DEPTH-3:DEPTH-1]};
            bins full_c     = {DEPTH};
        }
        cp_ops : coverpoint {wr_en, rd_en} {
            bins idle       = {2'b00};
            bins read_only  = {2'b01};
            bins write_only = {2'b10};
            bins both       = {2'b11};      // simultaneous - the interesting one
        }
        cross cp_occupancy, cp_ops;         // full AND writing; empty AND reading
    endgroup

    cg_fifo cov = new();

    //--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 6. Stimulus - the SAD paths, deliberately. Note the backpressure and the
    //    reset in the middle, which is where the bugs are.
    //--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    initial begin
        cb.wr_en   <= 1'b0;
        cb.rd_en   <= 1'b0;
        repeat (4) @(cb);
        rst_n = 1'b1;

        // Phase 1: fill it completely, including a write attempt while full.
        repeat (DEPTH + 4) begin
            @(cb);
            cb.wr_en   <= !full;
            cb.wr_data <= $urandom();
        end

        // Phase 2: drain it completely, including a read attempt while empty.
        @(cb); cb.wr_en <= 1'b0;
        repeat (DEPTH + 4) begin
            @(cb);
            cb.rd_en <= !empty;
        end

        // Phase 3: random concurrent traffic - the case that finds pointer bugs.
        repeat (10_000) begin
            @(cb);
            cb.wr_en   <= ($urandom_range(0,99) < 60) && !full;
            cb.rd_en   <= ($urandom_range(0,99) < 55) && !empty;
            cb.wr_data <= $urandom();
        end

        // Phase 4: reset in the middle of traffic. Almost nobody tests this,
        // and it is where "works in sim, hangs in hardware" comes from.
        @(cb); rst_n = 1'b0;
        model.delete();
        repeat (4) @(cb); rst_n = 1'b1;

        repeat (1000) begin
            @(cb);
            cb.wr_en   <= ($urandom_range(0,99) < 50) && !full;
            cb.rd_en   <= ($urandom_range(0,99) < 50) && !empty;
            cb.wr_data <= $urandom();
        end

        //----------------------------------------------------------------------
        // 7. The verdict. A testbench that does not decide is not a testbench.
        //----------------------------------------------------------------------
        $display("checked %0d beats, coverage %0.1f%%", beats_checked, cov.get_coverage());
        if (errors != 0) begin
            $display("TEST FAILED: %0d mismatch(es)", errors);
            $fatal(1);
        end
        if (cov.get_coverage() < 95.0) begin
            $display("TEST FAILED: coverage %0.1f%% below goal", cov.get_coverage());
            $fatal(1);
        end
        $display("TEST PASSED");
        $finish;
    end

endmodule

The last block is the one people leave out. A testbench that prints results and exits zero cannot be run by CI, so it will be run by a human, occasionally, who will read the log optimistically. Make the testbench decide, and make failure an exit status.

docs.title: Sharpen Your Pencil
docs.text:
1. Your functional coverage model has 120 bins and your generator is uniform random. Estimate the number of transactions needed to hit all of them. If each transaction is 50 cycles at 5,000 cycles/second of simulation, how long does that take?
  2. Your testbench passes. Then you add assert property (@(posedge clk) $onehot(state)) and it still passes. What has that told you, and what has it not?
  3. A block simulates perfectly and fails in hardware at reset. Name the three checks you would run, in order, and say which of them RTL simulation structurally cannot perform.

docs.title: Final Thoughts on the Sandbox
docs.text: Verification is the unsung hero of FPGA design. It’s not as "cool" as writing high-speed RTL, but it’s what separates the professionals from the amateurs. Build a robust, self-checking virtual lab. Map your coverage. Test the sad paths. If you can conquer the digital sandbox, the hardware lab will be a walk in the park.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
Brain Power — Simulation passes, hardware fails. Top three things to check?

1. Constraints, not RTL. Simulation has no concept of timing closure. If the hardware fails intermittently, at temperature, or on some boards and not others, the first suspect is a path that is not meeting timing or — much more often — a path that was never analysed. Run check_timing -verbose and report_timing_summary -report_unconstrained, and look for no_clock and unconstrained_internal_endpoints. RTL simulation is structurally incapable of finding this class of bug, because it has no delays.

2. Asynchronous inputs and clock domain crossings. Simulation drives your asynchronous inputs from a testbench that is, itself, synchronous — so the input changes neatly between edges and never lands in the aperture. Real hardware has no such courtesy. Run report_cdc -details and treat Critical findings as bugs (Section 2.3). Set ASYNC_REG TRUE on your synchronizers, which additionally makes simulation start modelling metastability instead of hiding it.

3. Reset and power-up state. Two distinct sub-problems. First, X-propagation: simulation may initialise a register to X and your logic may accidentally depend on X-pessimism or X-optimism, whereas real flops come out of configuration at their INIT value. Second, reset release: if reset deasserts asynchronously, different parts of the design leave reset in different cycles, and a state machine can start in an illegal state. This is the classic "works in simulation, hangs on the bench" and it is why xpm_cdc_sync_rst exists.

A useful fourth, if the failure is on the very first board: check that what you simulated is what you built. IP that is locked or out of date, a testbench instantiating a different parameterisation, or a top level that differs from the synthesised one all produce this exact symptom.

Sharpen Your Pencil #1 — 120 bins, uniform random:

\[E[n] \approx N(\ln N + \gamma) = 120 \times (\ln 120 + 0.5772) = 120 \times (4.787 + 0.577) = 120 \times 5.364 \approx 644\]

About 644 transactions on average. At 50 cycles each:

\[644 \times 50 = 32{,}200\ \text{cycles} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{32{,}200}{5000} = 6.4\ \text{seconds}\]

Trivial — which is the real lesson. Coverage closure on a well-sized model is cheap; it is the badly-sized model that is expensive. If your answer had come out in hours, the correct response would not be "run it overnight" but "my coverage model has too many bins," and the fix is to group values into equivalence classes that reflect what the design actually distinguishes.

Note also the difference between the mean and the tail: the last few bins take disproportionately long under pure random, so budget 2–3× the mean, or use coverage feedback to steer the generator once you are above ~90 %.

Sharpen Your Pencil #2 — The assertion passing tells you less than it appears to.

What it has told you: across all the stimulus you happened to run, the state register was never observed in a non-one-hot encoding.

What it has not told you:

  • That the assertion can ever fail. An assertion that is never reached under meaningful conditions passes vacuously. If your stimulus never drives the design into the corner where two state bits could be set, the assertion is decoration.
  • That your state machine is one-hot at all. If synthesis chose a binary encoding (which it will, unless you set FSM_ENCODING), the property may be checking a register whose encoding does not match your assumption — and passing for the wrong reason.
  • That illegal transitions do not occur. $onehot checks the state, not the sequence. A machine that jumps from IDLE directly to DONE, skipping the work, is one-hot at every instant.

What to do about it: check the assertion's coverage, not just its pass status. Most simulators report how many times each property was attempted and how many times it was vacuously satisfied. An assertion with zero non-vacuous attempts is a line of code that does nothing. And add the sequence property you actually meant:

assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (state == IDLE) |=> (state == IDLE || state == FETCH))
    else $error("illegal transition out of IDLE");

Sharpen Your Pencil #3 — Block simulates perfectly, fails in hardware at reset. In order:

  1. report_cdc -details, looking specifically at the reset paths. The most likely cause is asynchronous reset release: reset deasserts at an arbitrary point relative to the clock, different registers leave reset in different cycles, and the state machine starts in a state your RTL believes unreachable. RTL simulation can in principle find this, but only if the testbench deliberately deasserts reset asynchronously — and almost none do, because they release it on a clock edge.
  2. check_timing -verbose, looking for no_clock and unconstrained endpoints on the reset network, plus recovery/removal checks. A reset that is not timed can arrive anywhere.
  3. Gate-level simulation with SDF, targeted at reset only — a few hundred cycles, not a regression. This is the one that RTL simulation structurally cannot perform, because it requires real delays: recovery and removal violations, and X-propagation through the actual synthesised netlist rather than through your source's initialisers.

The structural answer to the question asked: RTL simulation cannot check timing. It has no delay model, so recovery/removal, setup/hold, and any failure whose mechanism is "the signal arrived at the wrong moment" is invisible to it by construction. That is not a weakness to work around; it is the reason static timing analysis and CDC analysis exist as separate tools, and why passing simulation is a necessary and thoroughly insufficient condition.

docs.title: There Are No Dumb Questions
docs.text:
Q: Do I need UVM?

A: For a block with a handful of interfaces and a clear reference model — no. The testbench above has a scoreboard, assertions, functional coverage and a verdict, and it is one file. UVM earns its complexity when you need reusable verification components across many blocks and many projects, constrained-random sequences with layered control, and a team large enough that the standardisation is worth the learning curve. Reaching for UVM on a single FIFO is how verification gets a reputation for being slow.

Q: What is the difference between code coverage and functional coverage?

A: Code coverage asks "did every line, branch and expression execute?" — it is generated automatically from your RTL and it is a measure of how much of what you wrote you exercised. Functional coverage asks "did every scenario I care about occur?" — you write it by hand, and it measures how much of what you meant you exercised. 100 % code coverage with no functional coverage means you executed every line of a design that might implement the wrong thing. You need both, and functional coverage is the one that requires thought.

Q: My assertion fires but I think the design is right. What now?

A: One of three things is true, and it is worth determining which rather than commenting out the assertion: the design is wrong; the assertion is wrong; or the specification is ambiguous and you and the assertion's author interpreted it differently. The third is the most valuable outcome, because you have just found a specification bug at simulation time rather than at integration. Disabling an assertion without resolving which case you are in is the single most expensive shortcut in verification.

Q: How do I test a reset that happens mid-transaction?

A: Deliberately, as in Phase 4 of the artifact above — and asynchronously, at a random offset within the clock period, not aligned to an edge. Then check that the DUT and your reference model return to the same state. Most reset bugs are not "reset does not work" but "reset works, and the two sides of an interface disagree about whether it happened."

Q: Is gate-level simulation obsolete now that static timing analysis is good?

A: Mostly, for timing — STA covers far more paths, far faster, and exhaustively. GLS remains worth its cost for three specific things: X-propagation at power-up and reset, verifying that synthesis did not change behaviour (especially where you have used DONT_TOUCH, black boxes, or hand-instantiated primitives), and asynchronous interfaces whose behaviour depends on real delays. Run it targeted at those questions, not as a regression.

docs.title: Bullet Points
docs.text:
• Coupon collector: hitting all \(N\) coverage bins by uniform random takes \(\approx N(\ln N + \gamma)\) transactions, not \(N\). 48 bins → ~214 transactions.
  • If your bin count is astronomically large, no simulation will close it. Redefine the model around equivalence classes, or use formal.
  • GLS is ~100× slower than RTL. 4 million cycles: 13 minutes RTL, 22 hours GLS. Use GLS for targeted questions, never for regression.
  • The four parts of a real testbench: clocking block (no races), reference model, scoreboard, assertions. Plus a verdict and a non-zero exit status.
  • Drive stimulus with <= after the edge; sample just before it. A clocking block states both. Bare # delays in stimulus race the DUT.
  • Assertions can pass vacuously. Check assertion coverage, not just pass status.
  • Test the sad paths: backpressure, full/empty boundaries, simultaneous read/write, and reset in the middle of traffic.
  • RTL simulation cannot check timing — no delay model. Recovery/removal, setup/hold and CDC failures are invisible to it by construction. check_timing, report_cdc and STA are not optional extras.

docs.title: Section 4.1: Synthesis Strategies: The Alchemist's Forge
docs.text: Synthesis is the moment of truth. It’s where your beautiful, abstract HDL code is melted down and forged into a physical netlist of gates, lookup tables (LUTs), and flip-flops. In the AMD UltraFast Methodology, synthesis is not just a push-button process; it’s an alchemical art. If you give the synthesis engine the right "ingredients" (attributes and settings), you’ll get a design that is fast and efficient. Give it the wrong ones, and you’ll end up with a mess of "logic sludge" that will never meet timing.

docs.title: The Alchemist's forge: Transforming Logic
docs.text:
The goal of synthesis is to find the best physical implementation for your logic. Vivado has several "Strategies" you can choose from. Most people start with the Default strategy, which is a good balance of speed and area. But if you’re pushing the limits of your FPGA, you might need to use Flow_PerfOptimized_high or Flow_AreaOptimized_high.

Think of these strategies like different recipes. One might focus on making the logic as fast as possible by adding extra registers (Pipelining), while another might focus on making it as small as possible by sharing resources. Choosing the right strategy early on can save you hours of implementation time later.

Brain Power If you use a "Performance Optimized" strategy, will your design use more or fewer LUTs than the "Area Optimized" version? Why might a "Performance Optimized" design actually be easier to route?

docs.title: The DONT_TOUCH Trap: Letting the Tools Work
docs.text:
A common mistake for experienced designers is using the DONT_TOUCH attribute on everything. They think they know better than the tool, so they "lock" their signals to prevent the synthesis engine from optimizing them. In the AMD UltraFast world, this is a dangerous game.

DONT_TOUCH prevents the tool from performing "Logic Optimization." If the tool sees two identical pieces of logic, it can't merge them. If it sees a signal that is constant, it can't remove it. This creates "Optimization Debt" that clogs up the routing engine. Use DONT_TOUCH sparingly, and only when you have a very specific reason to keep a signal alive (like for an ILA probe).

docs.title: Fireside Chat: The RTL Coder and the Synthesis Expert
docs.text:
RTL Coder: "My synthesis report says I'm using 80% of the LUTs on the chip! I haven't even added the PCIe core yet. What happened?"

Synthesis Expert: "Let me see your resets. Ah, here it is. You’re resetting every single counter and register in your data path. Because of those resets, the synthesis engine can't use the dedicated SRL16 resources. It’s building everything out of LUTs and flip-flops."

RTL Coder: "But I need those resets! What if the system glitches?"

Synthesis Expert: "You only need to reset the control logic. Let the data path be uninitialized. If you remove those unnecessary resets, the synthesis engine can pack your logic into Shift Register LUTs (SRLs). You’ll drop from 80% utilization to 20% in five minutes. Stop being a 'reset-happy' coder and start being a hardware architect."

docs.title: Control Set Optimization: Packing the Slices
docs.text:
AMD FPGAs organize flip-flops into groups called Slices. To fit into a slice, flip-flops must share the same Control Set (Clock, Reset, and Clock Enable). If your code has a chaotic mix of different resets and enables, the synthesis engine has to scatter your flip-flops across multiple slices, which wastes space and creates long wires.

The UltraFast methodology recommends Control Set Reduction. By minimizing the number of unique resets and enables, you allow the tools to pack your logic tightly. Think of it like packing a suitcase. If everything is the same shape, it’s easy. If everything is a different shape, you’re going to have a lot of wasted space.

docs.title: Timing-Driven Synthesis: The Critical Path
docs.text:
Vivado is a Timing-Driven tool. It looks at your XDC constraints (which we discussed in Chapter 2) and prioritizes the logic paths that are closest to failing their timing requirements. If a path has plenty of "slack," the tool will optimize it for area. If a path is "tight," the tool will pull out all the stops to make it fast.

This is why accurate constraints are so important. If you tell the tool that a 100MHz clock is actually 500MHz, the synthesis engine will waste all its energy trying to make that logic super-fast, potentially ruining the timing for the rest of your design. Be honest with the tools, and they will be honest with you.

docs.title: Code Detective: The Flattening Mystery
docs.text:
By default, Vivado maintains your design's hierarchy. But you can tell it to "Flatten" the design using the -flatten_hierarchy setting.

# Code Detective: Why might 'rebuilt' flattening be better than 'full'?
synth_design -top top_module -part xcku040-ffva1156-2-e -flatten_hierarchy full
# Hint: What happens to your signal names when you use 'full' flattening?

The flaw with full flattening is that it destroys your hierarchy and renames your signals to random strings of characters. This makes it impossible to debug using an ILA. The rebuilt setting is often a better choice—it allows the synthesis engine to optimize across hierarchical boundaries but "rebuilds" the hierarchy at the end so you can still find your signals.

There is a second cost that matters more than debug convenience: flattened designs lose the hierarchy that the placer and report_utilization -hierarchical reason about. You give up the ability to answer "which module is burning the LUTs?" and you give up KEEP_HIERARCHY as a floorplanning lever, in exchange for optimisation across boundaries that rebuilt gives you anyway.

The fix:

# Corrected: cross-boundary optimisation without losing your names.
synth_design -top top_module -part xcku040-ffva1156-2-e \
    -flatten_hierarchy rebuilt \
    -directive Default

# Then keep the boundaries you specifically need for debug or floorplanning.
# KEEP_HIERARCHY blocks optimisation ACROSS that boundary, so use it deliberately:
#   - on a module you intend to pblock
#   - on a module you intend to probe with an ILA
#   - on a module you have characterised and do not want re-optimised
# and not as a blanket setting, or you will block the merging that saves you area.
set_property KEEP_HIERARCHY SOFT [get_cells u_dsp_pipeline]

# Verify you kept what you meant to keep:
report_utilization -hierarchical -hierarchical_depth 3 -file util_hier.rpt

KEEP_HIERARCHY SOFT is the useful middle setting: the boundary survives synthesis for reporting and constraint purposes, but implementation may still optimise through it. TRUE is the hard version, and it costs real QoR — measure before you reach for it.

docs.title: Analogy → Silicon
docs.text: In the story In the silicon Where the analogy breaks The alchemist's forge synth_design mapping RTL onto LUT6, FDRE, CARRY8, DSP48E2, RAMB36E2 Alchemy is opaque; synthesis publishes its reasoning in the log and in report_qor_suggestions, and reading it is the skill Different recipes -directive values: Default, PerformanceOptimized_high, AreaOptimized_high, RuntimeOptimized Recipes give predictably different dishes; directives are heuristics, and a "performance" directive can produce worse QoR on your specific design — you must measure Locking the ingredients DONT_TOUCH / KEEP / MARK_DEBUG Locking one ingredient is local; DONT_TOUCH blocks optimisation through the object, so it propagates outward and can cost far more than the object itself Packing a suitcase Control set reduction and CLB packing Suitcase items compress; control sets are exact — see the arithmetic in Section 3.1 Being honest with the tools Timing-driven synthesis using your XDC to prioritise Honesty is binary; over-constraining is a specific failure mode where the tool optimises the wrong paths and starves the real ones

docs.title: Do the Math
docs.text: Synthesis decisions are a resource trade you can compute rather than guess.

docs.title: What over-constraining actually costs
docs.text:
Timing-driven synthesis allocates effort in proportion to how close a path is to failing. Suppose your design has a genuine 100 MHz control domain and a 400 MHz datapath, and someone constrains the control clock at 400 MHz "for margin."

Givens:

Quantity Value Control domain flops 20,000 Datapath flops 60,000 Real control requirement 10.000 ns Constrained as 2.500 ns

The control logic now appears to need a 4× speed-up it does not need. Synthesis responds by replicating high-fanout drivers, unpacking control sets to shorten paths, and duplicating logic — all of which cost area:

\[\text{Effort misdirected} = \frac{20{,}000}{80{,}000} = 25\ \%\ \text{of the design}\]

And that effort comes out of the datapath's budget, which is where you actually needed it. The observable symptoms are characteristic: utilisation climbs, runtime climbs, congestion appears in a region that was previously fine, and the datapath's WNS gets worse after you tightened an unrelated constraint. Over-constraining is not free margin; it is a reallocation of a fixed effort budget away from the paths that matter.

docs.title: Directive sweeps: what they cost and what they are worth
docs.text:
Givens:

Quantity Value Synthesis runtime 25 minutes Implementation runtime 3 hours Directives worth trying 4 synth × 5 impl

A full cross product is \(4 \times 5 = 20\) runs:

\[20 \times (0.42 + 3)\ \text{hours} = 68\ \text{hours}\]

Nearly three days of machine time — feasible on a build farm, absurd on a laptop, and in either case worth doing only after you know what is failing. A directive sweep is a search over heuristics; if your problem is 11 levels of logic on a path, no heuristic will fix it and you have spent three days confirming that.

The disciplined order:

  1. Diagnose with report_design_analysis and report_qor_suggestions — minutes.
  2. Fix what the diagnosis names: pipelining, fanout, control sets, floorplan — hours, and it usually moves WNS by hundreds of picoseconds.
  3. Then sweep directives to recover the last tens of picoseconds — days, for a payoff measured in tens of picoseconds.

Doing this in reverse order is the single most common way to waste a week of timing closure.

docs.title: The Real Artifact
docs.text:
A synthesis script that records why each setting is there, plus the reports that tell you whether it worked. Scripts without this commentary become cargo cult within one project handover.

#==============================================================================
# synth.tcl - synthesis with reasons attached.
#
# Rule of the file: every non-default setting carries a comment saying what
# measurement motivated it. A setting whose justification nobody remembers is
# a setting that gets copied into the next project and slowly makes it worse.
#==============================================================================

set part      xcku040-ffva1156-2-e
set top       top_module
set build_dir ./build

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. SYNTHESIS
#
#   -flatten_hierarchy rebuilt : optimise across boundaries, keep the names.
#                                Never 'full' - you lose ILA probing and
#                                hierarchical utilisation reporting.
#   -directive                 : start at Default. Only change it once
#                                report_qor_suggestions says the bottleneck is
#                                something a directive addresses.
#   -retiming                  : lets synthesis move registers across logic to
#                                balance stages. Cheap win on pipelined datapaths;
#                                it does NOT add registers, only relocates them.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
synth_design -top $top -part $part \
    -flatten_hierarchy rebuilt \
    -directive Default \
    -retiming

write_checkpoint -force $build_dir/post_synth.dcp

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. THE FOUR REPORTS THAT DIAGNOSE SYNTHESIS QoR
#    Read them in this order. Each answers a different question.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Q: Did I get the hard blocks I expected, and which module burned the fabric?
report_utilization -hierarchical -hierarchical_depth 3 \
    -file $build_dir/util_hier.rpt

# Q: Is my control set count sane? (See Section 3.1 for the arithmetic.)
#    The summary at the top is the number to track release over release.
report_control_sets -verbose -file $build_dir/control_sets.rpt

# Q: What does Vivado itself think is wrong, and what would it do?
#    This is the highest-value report in the flow and the least used. It names
#    specific cells and specific fixes, and it can emit machine-readable
#    suggestions that implementation will act on.
report_qor_suggestions -file $build_dir/qor_suggestions.rpt
write_qor_suggestions -force $build_dir/qor.rqs

# Q: Am I about to fight congestion or complexity?
report_design_analysis -complexity -congestion \
    -file $build_dir/design_analysis.rpt

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. ATTRIBUTE HYGIENE
#    Audit these every release. DONT_TOUCH accumulates: each one was added for a
#    reason that expired, and collectively they strangle optimisation.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
proc audit_optimization_blockers {} {
    set report {}
    foreach attr {DONT_TOUCH KEEP KEEP_HIERARCHY MARK_DEBUG} {
        set cells [get_cells -hier -quiet -filter "$attr"]
        set nets  [get_nets  -hier -quiet -filter "$attr"]
        set n [expr {[llength $cells] + [llength $nets]}]
        if {$n > 0} {
            lappend report [format "  %-16s %4d object(s)" $attr $n]
        }
    }
    if {[llength $report]} {
        puts "Optimisation blockers present:"
        puts [join $report "\n"]
        puts "Each one blocks merging, constant propagation and retiming through it."
        puts "Justify or remove. MARK_DEBUG in particular must not reach production."
    } else {
        puts "No optimisation blockers set."
    }
}
audit_optimization_blockers

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. FEED THE SUGGESTIONS BACK IN
#    The .rqs file from step 2 is not documentation - implementation consumes it.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# read_qor_suggestions $build_dir/qor.rqs
# opt_design -directive ExploreWithRemap

docs.title: Sharpen Your Pencil
docs.text:
1. report_control_sets reports 3,100 unique control sets against 24,000 flip-flops. Using the CLB model from Section 3.1, estimate the CLB cost versus the ideal, and say what you would look for in the RTL.
  2. Your synthesis run reports 40 % LUT utilisation. After adding DONT_TOUCH to twelve modules for ILA probing, it reports 58 %. Explain the mechanism, and say what you would do instead.
  3. You have a design failing timing by −0.400 ns with Logic Levels: 9 on the worst paths and route 22 %. You have three days. Allocate them across: directive sweep, RTL pipelining, and floorplanning. Justify the split.

docs.title: Final Thoughts on the Forge
docs.text: Synthesis is the bridge between the digital dream and the physical reality. By choosing the right strategies, minimizing DONT_TOUCH attributes, and optimizing your control sets, you give the synthesis engine the freedom it needs to build a world-class design. Respect the forge, and it will give you a design that is strong, lean, and fast.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
Brain Power — Performance-optimized vs area-optimized: more or fewer LUTs? Why might the performance version be easier to route?

More LUTs, usually — and sometimes substantially. Performance-oriented synthesis buys speed with area in three main ways:

  • Logic replication. A high-fanout driver is duplicated so each copy serves fewer loads over shorter wires. More LUTs, shorter nets.
  • Less resource sharing. Area optimisation will merge two multiplexers that are never used simultaneously into one with extra select logic; performance optimisation leaves them separate because the shared version has a longer path.
  • Retiming and restructuring, which can flatten a logic chain into a wider, shallower tree — fewer levels, more LUTs.

Why the larger design can be easier to route: routing difficulty is driven by wire demand in a region, not by LUT count. A replicated driver produces several short local nets instead of one long net crossing the die; a shallower logic tree produces shorter critical paths that the placer can satisfy with local resources. So you can add 8 % LUTs and reduce congestion, because the extra logic is spent buying locality.

The important caveat, and the reason the honest answer is "measure": this stops being true near the top of the device. At 90 % utilisation, extra LUTs mean the placer has nowhere to put the replicas, and performance optimisation makes both area and congestion worse. The directive that helps at 60 % utilisation can be the wrong one at 90 %.

Sharpen Your Pencil #1 — 3,100 control sets, 24,000 flops:

\[\frac{24{,}000}{3{,}100} = 7.7 \text{ flops per control set}\]

Each control set needs \(\lceil 7.7/8 \rceil = 1\) half-CLB, so:

\[\text{half-CLBs} = 3{,}100 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{CLBs} = 1{,}550\]

Ideal: \(24{,}000 / 16 = 1{,}500\) CLBs.

So this design is at 1,550 versus 1,500 — only about 3 % overhead. This one is healthy, and that is the point of the exercise: 3,100 sounds like a large number, and the ratio is what matters, not the absolute count. Do not go refactoring RTL on the basis of a scary-looking total.

If the ratio had been poor (say 4 flops per set), the RTL patterns to look for are per-instance enables from generate loops, per-bit resets, and state machines computing a unique enable expression per destination register.

Sharpen Your Pencil #2 — 40 % → 58 % from twelve DONT_TOUCH attributes.

The mechanism, and it compounds:

  1. Blocked constant propagation. A DONT_TOUCH net whose driver is a constant can no longer be folded away, so all the logic downstream that would have collapsed survives.
  2. Blocked merging. Two identical modules that would have been merged into one now both exist.
  3. Blocked boundary optimisation. Unused outputs of a DONT_TOUCH module cannot be removed, which keeps alive the entire cone of logic feeding them — this is usually the biggest contributor and the least obvious.
  4. Blocked retiming and control set merging through the marked objects, which costs packing efficiency on top of the raw logic.

Twelve modules is enough for these to interact: logic kept alive in one module feeds another where it also cannot be optimised.

What to do instead: use MARK_DEBUG on the specific nets you want to probe rather than DONT_TOUCH on whole modules.

(* mark_debug = "true" *) logic [31:0] axi_wdata_probe;

MARK_DEBUG preserves the net for debug insertion with far narrower scope than a module-level DONT_TOUCH. Better still, use the ILA insertion flow on the synthesised netlist (set_property MARK_DEBUG true [get_nets ...] after synth_design), so the attributes never touch your source at all and cannot be forgotten before release. And whatever you use, run the audit_optimization_blockers proc from the artifact each release — the failure mode is not adding one, it is never removing it.

Sharpen Your Pencil #3 — −0.400 ns, Logic Levels: 9, route 22 %. Three days.

The diagnosis first, because it determines everything: route is only 22 %, so this is a logic-dominated failure. Nine levels is deep. The time budget follows from that:

  • Day 1 — RTL pipelining (≈70 % of the effort). Nine levels of logic is the disease; everything else is symptom management. Find the worst path group with report_timing -setup -max_paths 50 -path_type summary, identify the shared structure (it is usually one wide comparator, one priority encoder, or one arithmetic expression feeding many endpoints), and split it into two stages. A 9-level path becomes two 4–5-level paths, which at −0.400 ns is very likely all you need. Also try synth_design -retiming first, since it is one flag and it costs one synthesis run.
  • Day 2 — verify and re-close (≈20 %). Pipelining changes latency, so the protocol around it needs re-verification. This is real work and skipping it is how a timing fix becomes a functional bug. Re-run implementation and confirm the fix held.
  • Day 3 — directive sweep, only if still short (≈10 %). Now, and only now, is a sweep worth the machine time, because you are hunting the last tens of picoseconds, which is what directives are actually good for.

Floorplanning gets zero. With route at 22 % of the path, perfect placement recovers at most a fraction of that 22 %, against a 400 ps deficit driven by logic depth. Floorplanning is the right tool for the mirror-image problem (route 78 %, levels 3), and spending a day on it here would be a day spent confirming that.

docs.title: There Are No Dumb Questions
docs.text:
Q: Should I just try all the directives and keep whichever wins?

A: Eventually, yes — but not first. A sweep is a search over heuristics, and it typically moves WNS by tens of picoseconds. Diagnosis plus a targeted fix typically moves it by hundreds. Sweep when you are close, diagnose when you are not. The arithmetic in Do the Math shows a full cross product costs nearly three days of machine time; spend that after you know what you are buying.

Q: What is the difference between DONT_TOUCH and KEEP?

A: KEEP prevents a net from being optimised away but still allows optimisation around it. DONT_TOUCH prevents the object and everything through it from being optimised, and it propagates — putting it on a module protects the whole module's boundary. DONT_TOUCH is the heavier hammer and is what you want for structural things that must survive (synchronizer chains, SLR hop registers); KEEP is usually enough for keeping a signal visible.

Q: Does -retiming add pipeline stages for me?

A: No, and this is the most common misunderstanding of the flag. Retiming moves existing registers across combinational logic to balance the delay between stages. If your path has one register at each end and nine levels between them, retiming has nothing to move and will not help. It is excellent at fixing an unbalanced pipeline (2 levels then 7 levels becomes 4 and 5) and useless at fixing a shallow one. Add the register in RTL; let retiming place it well.

Q: My IP shows enormous utilisation in report_utilization -hierarchical. Is the IP bloated?

A: Check whether you flattened. With -flatten_hierarchy full, logic gets attributed to wherever it ended up, and hierarchical utilisation becomes meaningless. With rebuilt the numbers are trustworthy. If they are trustworthy and still large, check the IP's configuration — most AMD IP has options that trade area for features you may not be using (ECC, wider FIFOs, extra AXI channels).

Q: How do I know if I am over-constrained?

A: Compare the constraint against the requirement, not against the result. Run report_clocks and, for each clock, ask "what does this actually need to be?" A clock constrained faster than any external interface or internal throughput requirement demands is over-constrained. The symptom to watch for is utilisation and runtime rising while WNS on an unrelated domain gets worse — that is effort being drawn away from where you need it.

docs.title: Bullet Points
docs.text:
• -flatten_hierarchy rebuilt, not full. You keep cross-boundary optimisation and your signal names, ILA probing, and hierarchical utilisation reporting.
  • KEEP_HIERARCHY SOFT preserves a boundary for reporting and constraints without hard-blocking implementation. TRUE costs QoR — measure before using it.
  • Diagnose, fix, then sweep. Diagnosis is minutes and moves WNS by hundreds of ps; a full directive sweep is ~68 hours of machine time and moves it by tens.
  • -retiming relocates registers; it does not create them. It fixes unbalanced pipelines, not shallow ones.
  • Over-constraining reallocates a fixed effort budget away from the paths that need it. Symptom: utilisation and runtime up, unrelated WNS down.
  • DONT_TOUCH propagates and blocks constant propagation, merging and boundary optimisation. Use MARK_DEBUG on specific nets for debug, and audit blockers every release.
  • Performance directives usually cost LUTs and can still improve routability — until you are near full, where they make both worse.
  • The four synthesis reports, in order: report_utilization -hierarchical, report_control_sets -verbose, report_qor_suggestions (+ write_qor_suggestions), report_design_analysis -complexity -congestion.
