docs.title: Section 4.2: Placement and Routing: The Digital Tetris
docs.text:
If synthesis is the forge where your logic is created, then Placement and Routing (P&R) is the game of Digital Tetris where those pieces are fitted onto the physical silicon. In an AMD FPGA, you have millions of tiny "slots" (LUTs, registers, and interconnects). Your logic blocks need to be placed in these slots and then connected by a complex web of tiny copper wires.

This isn't just about making things fit; it's about making them fit perfectly. If two blocks that talk to each other are placed on opposite sides of the chip, the wire connecting them will be long and slow. In the high-speed world of FPGA design, every millimeter of wire adds nanoseconds of delay.

docs.title: Digital Tetris: The Physical Grid
docs.text:
The placement engine’s job is to group related logic together. It looks at your design and tries to keep "clusters" of logic in the same neighborhood. This is why a clean hierarchy (from Section 3.2) is so important—it gives the tool a hint about which blocks should stay together.

But sometimes, the "Tetris pieces" don't fit easily. If you have a design that is 95% full, the tool has almost no room to move things around. This leads to "Sub-optimal Placement," where the tool is forced to put critical components far apart just to make them fit. Aim for 70-80% utilization for a comfortable design; anything higher is playing Tetris on "Expert" mode.

Brain Power Why does a design with 99% utilization often fail timing, even if the logic itself is very simple? (Hint: Think about the routing 'channels' between the logic blocks.)

docs.title: Congestion: The Traffic Jam from Hell
docs.text:
Congestion is the number one enemy of routing. It happens when too many wires are trying to pass through the same narrow area of the chip. Imagine a ten-lane highway that suddenly narrows down to a single-lane bridge. That bridge is a "Congestion Hotspot."

When the routing engine hits a hotspot, it has to "detour" wires around the area. These detours make the wires longer, which increases delay and kills your timing. To avoid congestion, keep your logic modular and avoid "Global" signals that have to touch every single block. If you see congestion in your reports, you might need to spread your logic out manually.

docs.title: Fireside Chat: The Floorplanner and the Auto-Router
docs.text:
Floorplanner: "I’ve spent all morning creating PBLOCKs for the DSP engine. I’ve locked it down to the bottom-left corner of the chip to keep it away from the noisy PCIe interface."

Auto-Router: "That’s cute. But by locking that logic down, you’ve created a massive bottleneck at the edge of your PBLOCK. I’m trying to route 512 wires out of that corner, and there just isn't enough copper."

Floorplanner: "But if I don't lock it down, you'll scatter the logic all over the die and I’ll never meet my 400MHz target!"

Auto-Router: "I’m not a child. If you give me a 'Soft Constraint' instead of a 'Hard PBLOCK,' I can move things around just enough to clear the congestion while still keeping the logic relatively close together. Give me some breathing room, and I’ll give you a design that meets timing."

docs.title: SLR Crossings: The Great Divide
docs.text:
In larger AMD FPGAs (the "UltraScale+" family), the chip is actually made of multiple separate silicon dies called Super Logic Regions (SLRs). These dies are connected by a special high-speed bridge called a Super Long Line (SLL).

Crossing an SLR boundary is a big deal. It adds a significant amount of delay—equivalent to several nanoseconds. If you have a critical path that crosses an SLR, you must pipeline it. This means putting a register on both sides of the boundary to "catch" the data and give the tools a full clock cycle to make the jump. Ignore this, and the "Great Divide" will swallow your timing whole.

docs.title: PBLOCKS: The Zoning Laws of Silicon
docs.text:
Sometimes the auto-placement engine needs a little help. PBLOCKs (Physical Blocks) are manual constraints where you tell Vivado, "This specific module must stay within this specific rectangular area of the silicon."

Think of PBLOCKs as zoning laws. You’re telling the tool where the "Industrial Zone" (the high-speed math) and the "Residential Zone" (the slow control logic) should be. PBLOCKs are powerful, but they are also dangerous. If you make a PBLOCK too small, you create congestion. If you make it too big, you waste area. Use them as a last resort when the auto-tools are failing.

docs.title: Code Detective: The Unbuffered Clock
docs.text:
A common routing disaster is an "Unbuffered Clock." In an FPGA, clocks must use dedicated "Global Clock" lines.

# Code Detective: Why will this lead to a routing failure?
set_property PACKAGE_PIN A10 [get_ports my_clock]
# No BUFG or IBUFG instantiated in the HDL...

The flaw here is that the clock signal is being treated like a regular data signal. Instead of using the dedicated, low-skew high-speed clock network, the tool will try to route the clock through the regular "fabric" wires. This creates massive Clock Skew, where different parts of your design see the clock edge at different times.

In practice Vivado will usually stop you rather than let you ship it, and the error it produces is one worth recognising on sight:

ERROR: [Place 30-574] Poor placement for routing between an IO pin and BUFG.
  If this sub optimal condition is acceptable for this design, you may use the
  CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE constraint in the .xdc file to demote this message to
  a WARNING...

That message means the clock-capable pin you chose is not in a clock region that can reach the BUFGCE the placer wants to use. The temptation is to paste the constraint the error message suggests. Do not. Demoting the message tells the tool to route your clock through fabric anyway — you have silenced the alarm, not fixed the fault.

The fix, in order of preference:

// 1. Best: bring the clock in on a clock-capable (CC) pin and buffer it explicitly.
IBUFDS u_ibuf (.I(sys_clk_p), .IB(sys_clk_n), .O(clk_ibuf));
BUFGCE u_bufg (.I(clk_ibuf), .CE(1'b1), .O(clk));

# 2. Confirm the pin you chose is actually clock-capable, BEFORE the board is built:
#    IS_GLOBAL_CLK is the property that matters.
get_property IS_GLOBAL_CLK [get_package_pins A10]

# 3. Only if the board is already fabricated and the pin is wrong is the constraint
#    justified - and then it is a documented compromise, not a fix:
#    set_property CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE FALSE [get_nets my_clock]
#    Record the measured skew in the design documentation so the next person knows
#    the timing report is optimistic.

# 4. Verify what you actually got:
report_clock_networks -file clk_networks.rpt
#    Every clock should show a BUFG-class driver. A clock whose driver is a LUT or
#    an IBUF is being routed through fabric.

The general principle: an error message that offers you a constraint to silence it is describing a trade, not a solution. Read what you would be trading away before you accept.

docs.title: Analogy → Silicon
docs.text: In the story In the silicon Where the analogy breaks Digital Tetris place_design assigning cells to CLB/DSP/BRAM sites Tetris pieces are rigid and the board is empty at the start; placement is a continuous optimisation over a partly-constrained device, and "fits" is not the goal — "fits with slack" is Ten lanes narrowing to one Routing congestion: demand for interconnect exceeding supply in a region Traffic redistributes over time; routing demand is fixed by your netlist, so a congested region does not clear — it fails, or it detours and costs you timing Zoning laws Pblocks (create_pblock, resize_pblock) Zoning constrains what may be built; a pblock constrains where, and an over-tight one manufactures the congestion it was meant to prevent The great divide SLR boundaries crossed via SLLs and Laguna registers A divide is a line on a map; this one has a fixed resource budget and a delay you must budget a whole cycle for (Section 1.4) Soft constraint vs hard PBLOCK CONTAIN_ROUTING / EXCLUDE_PLACEMENT off vs on "Soft" sounds like a weaker version of the same thing; it is a different thing — it lets the placer relieve pressure at the edges, which is usually what makes the pblock work at all

docs.title: Utilisation versus routability: why 99 % fails and 75 % does not
docs.text:
Each CLB has a finite number of routing tracks entering and leaving it. Placement fills logic sites; routing consumes interconnect, and the two run out at different points.

Givens — a simplified model that captures the effect:

Quantity Value Logic sites in a region 1,000 CLBs Routing tracks available per region 24,000 track-segments Average track-segments consumed per placed CLB 20

At 75 % logic utilisation:

\[750\ \text{CLBs} \times 20 = 15{,}000\ \text{track-segments} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{15{,}000}{24{,}000} = 63\ \%\ \text{routing demand}\]

At 99 %:

\[990 \times 20 = 19{,}800 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{19{,}800}{24{,}000} = 83\ \%\]

83 % does not sound fatal — but routing demand is not uniform, and this is the part the average hides. The router must detour whenever a local hotspot exceeds 100 %, and each detour lengthens a net, which consumes yet more track-segments, which pushes neighbouring regions toward their own limit. The failure is super-linear: at 63 % average demand a hotspot at 1.5× the average is still routable; at 83 % the same hotspot is at 125 % and must detour, and its detours push its neighbours over too.

That is why the practical guidance is a utilisation band rather than a limit:

Logic utilisation What to expect < 70 % Placement and routing are not your problem. Look elsewhere. 70–85 % Normal. Congestion is manageable with directives and modest floorplanning. 85–90 % Every run gets slower, results get noisier, incremental changes have non-local effects. > 90 % You are buying timing closure with engineering weeks. Consider a bigger device — it is usually cheaper than the schedule.

docs.title: Reading congestion levels
docs.text:
report_design_analysis -congestion reports congestion on a 1–8 scale per region, for both placement and routing. The scale is logarithmic in the window size the router had to search:

Level Meaning Action 1–2 Nothing to see — 3–4 Mild, localised Usually resolves itself; note it and move on 5–6 Real congestion Act: reduce fanout, spread logic, revisit a pblock 7–8 Severe Routing will likely fail or timing will collapse. Architectural fix needed.

Level 5 is the threshold that matters. Below it, spend your time on timing; at or above it, congestion is your timing problem and fixing paths individually will not help.

docs.title: The Real Artifact
docs.text:
Congestion diagnosis, then a pblock that helps rather than hurts. Both are scripts you keep, not steps you remember.

#==============================================================================
# congestion_triage.tcl - run after place_design, before you change anything.
#
# The mistake this script exists to prevent: reacting to a congested design by
# tightening pblocks. Tight pblocks CAUSE congestion. Diagnose first.
#==============================================================================

proc congestion_triage {} {
    puts "\n=== 1. Where is it congested, and how badly? ==="
    # Levels are 1-8 per region for placement and routing. >= 5 needs action.
    report_design_analysis -congestion -name congestion

    puts "\n=== 2. Is it complexity (Rent exponent) or just density? ==="
    # A high Rent exponent means the netlist itself is highly interconnected -
    # that is an RTL problem, and no placement directive will fix it.
    report_design_analysis -complexity -name complexity

    puts "\n=== 3. High-fanout nets are the most common single cause ==="
    report_high_fanout_nets -timing -load_types -max_nets 25

    puts "\n=== 4. Did any pblock become the bottleneck? ==="
    foreach pb [get_pblocks -quiet] {
        set cells [get_cells -quiet -of_objects $pb]
        set stats [report_utilization -pblocks $pb -return_string]
        puts "  pblock [get_property NAME $pb]: [llength $cells] cell(s)"
        puts "    (check the CLB row of this report - over ~80% inside a pblock is"
        puts "     where a floorplan starts working against you)"
    }

    puts "\n=== 5. What does Vivado suggest? ==="
    report_qor_suggestions -max_paths 10
}

congestion_triage

#==============================================================================
# floorplan.xdc - a pblock that helps.
#
# Four rules, learned expensively:
#   1. Size it from measured utilisation, not from intuition. Target <= 70%
#      utilisation INSIDE the pblock, because the placer needs slack to route.
#   2. Leave CONTAIN_ROUTING false unless you have proven you need it. Containing
#      routing inside a tight boundary is the fastest way to manufacture congestion.
#   3. Align to CLOCKREGION boundaries. A pblock that cuts a clock region in half
#      splits the clock tree and buys you skew you did not want.
#   4. Constrain the module that has a REASON to be somewhere - next to its I/O,
#      next to its memory controller, inside one SLR. Do not pblock logic just
#      because it is large.
#==============================================================================

# The transceiver-facing datapath must live near its GT sites. That is the reason.
create_pblock pblk_gt_datapath
add_cells_to_pblock pblk_gt_datapath [get_cells -hier -filter {NAME =~ "*u_gt_rx_path*"}]
resize_pblock pblk_gt_datapath -add CLOCKREGION_X0Y2:CLOCKREGION_X1Y5

# Soft by default: the placer may spill at the edges to relieve pressure.
set_property CONTAIN_ROUTING    false [get_pblocks pblk_gt_datapath]
set_property EXCLUDE_PLACEMENT  false [get_pblocks pblk_gt_datapath]

# Check the size is right, every run:
#   report_utilization -pblocks [get_pblocks pblk_gt_datapath]
# If CLB utilisation inside the pblock exceeds ~70%, GROW IT. A pblock at 90%
# is a congestion generator, and it will make the design worse than no pblock.

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Fanout control - cheaper and more effective than floorplanning, and the first
# thing to try when report_high_fanout_nets names a culprit.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Replicate the driver of a high-fanout control net so each copy serves a
# local group. 'MAX_FANOUT' asks synthesis to do it for you:
set_property MAX_FANOUT 200 [get_nets u_ctrl/global_enable]

# For resets specifically, prefer a proper reset tree in RTL over MAX_FANOUT -
# a replicated reset whose copies deassert in different cycles is a new bug.

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Implementation directives that specifically target congestion. Try in this
# order; each is one implementation run.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#   place_design    -directive AltSpreadLogic_high
#   place_design    -directive SSI_SpreadLogic_high     (SSI devices)
#   phys_opt_design -directive AggressiveExplore
#   route_design    -directive AlternateCLBRouting

docs.title: Sharpen Your Pencil
docs.text:
1. report_design_analysis -congestion reports level 6 placement congestion in one clock region, and your design is at 68 % overall LUT utilisation. What does the combination of those two numbers tell you, and what would you check first?
  2. A pblock containing 4,000 CLBs' worth of logic is sized at 4,200 CLBs. Compute the utilisation inside it and say whether it will help or hurt.
  3. You get [Place 30-574] on a design whose board is already fabricated with the clock on a non-clock-capable pin. Write down what you will do and what you will document.

docs.title: Final Thoughts on the Grid
docs.text: Placement and Routing is where the "rubber meets the road." It’s the final test of your design's physical viability. By respecting congestion, pipelining SLR crossings, and using PBLOCKs wisely, you turn the "Digital Tetris" into a winning game. Keep your logic modular, give the tools some room to breathe, and watch your design slide perfectly into place.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
Brain Power — Why does a 99 % utilised design fail timing even when the logic is simple?

Because logic sites and routing resources run out at different rates, and timing is paid for out of the second one.

At 99 % logic utilisation the placer has essentially no freedom. Two cells that want to be adjacent get placed wherever there is a hole, which may be a long way apart. Then the router, which has almost no spare track-segments in that region, cannot take the direct path either — so it detours. Each detour lengthens a net, and a longer net both costs delay directly and consumes more track-segments, raising demand for every other net in the region. The effect is super-linear, which is why 90 % feels manageable and 99 % feels like a wall.

Concretely, the same simple logic that routes in 200 ps at 70 % utilisation may route in 900 ps at 99 %, and there is no RTL change that addresses it — the netlist was never the problem.

There is a second, subtler mechanism worth knowing: at extreme utilisation the placer starts making packing compromises, putting flops with different control sets into suboptimal arrangements and spreading what should be a tight cluster across several CLBs. So even the "simple logic" gets physically larger than it needed to be.

The practical conclusion: utilisation is a timing parameter, not just a capacity parameter. If you are above 90 % and fighting timing, price a bigger device against the engineering weeks. The device is usually cheaper.

Sharpen Your Pencil #1 — Level 6 congestion at 68 % overall utilisation.

The combination is the diagnostic. Overall utilisation is comfortable, so the design as a whole is not too big for the device — which means the congestion is local, not global. Something is concentrating interconnect demand in one region.

What to check, in order:

  1. report_high_fanout_nets -timing -load_types. A single net with thousands of loads whose driver sits in that region is the most common cause, and the cheapest to fix (MAX_FANOUT, or replication in RTL).
  2. report_design_analysis -complexity for that region. A high Rent exponent means the netlist in that region is intrinsically highly interconnected — a crossbar, a large multiplexer, a wide shared bus. That is an RTL problem, and placement directives will not fix it.
  3. Pblocks. If you have one covering or bordering that region, check its internal utilisation. A pblock at 90 % inside is a congestion generator even when the device is at 68 %.
  4. Hard block placement. A memory controller, transceiver bank or HBM interface at one edge pulls all its traffic through the fabric next to it. That congestion is structural, and the fix is floorplanning the consumers nearer to it.

What not to do: reach for a placement directive first. Directives redistribute congestion; they do not remove demand. Find what is generating the demand.

Sharpen Your Pencil #2 —

\[\frac{4{,}000}{4{,}200} = 95\ \%\ \text{utilisation inside the pblock}\]

It will hurt, badly. You have created a region at 95 % utilisation inside a device that may be comfortable everywhere else — precisely the condition from the Brain Power answer, except you built it deliberately. The placer has no room to arrange logic well inside the boundary, the router has no spare tracks, and every net that must leave the pblock has to squeeze through an edge that is also saturated.

The correct size, targeting ≤ 70 % inside:

\[\text{Required} = \frac{4{,}000}{0.70} \approx 5{,}715\ \text{CLBs}\]

So roughly 5,700–6,000 CLBs, aligned outward to clock region boundaries. And check it every run:

report_utilization -pblocks [get_pblocks pblk_name]

The general lesson: a pblock is a hint about locality, not a container you fill. If you find yourself sizing one tightly to "not waste area," you have misunderstood what it is for — the area inside a pblock is not consumed by the pblock, it is available to whatever the placer wants to put there, and leaving room is the entire point.

Sharpen Your Pencil #3 — [Place 30-574], board already fabricated, clock on a non-clock-capable pin.

What you will do:

  1. Verify the pin really is not clock-capable, rather than the placer simply having chosen a distant BUFGCE:

    get_property IS_GLOBAL_CLK [get_package_pins <pin>]

    If it is clock-capable, the fix is placement — constrain the BUFGCE to a clock region the pin can reach, and the error goes away legitimately.

  2. If it genuinely is not, accept the compromise explicitly:

    set_property CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE FALSE [get_nets my_clock]

    and immediately bound the damage: get the clock onto a BUFGCE as close to the pin as possible so only the pin-to-buffer segment is on fabric routing, not the whole tree.

  3. Measure the consequence. Run report_clock_networks and, more importantly, look at the clock skew reported on paths in that domain. Fabric routing on the input segment adds delay and, more dangerously, adds variation — which shows up as increased uncertainty on every path in that domain.

  4. Consider derating the interface. If this clock feeds a source-synchronous input, the extra insertion delay changes your input delay budget (Section 2.2). Recompute it.

What you will document, and this is the part that matters:

  • That CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE FALSE is present, on which net, and why — "board rev A routed the clock to pin X which is not clock-capable."
  • The measured skew and the timing margin lost.
  • A board change request for the next revision. The constraint is a workaround for a hardware defect, and if nobody records it as such, revision B will have the same pin assignment and the next engineer will find a mysterious constraint with no explanation.

That last bullet is the difference between a compromise and a landmine.

docs.title: There Are No Dumb Questions
docs.text:
Q: Should I floorplan every design?

A: No. Under about 70 % utilisation, on a single-SLR device, with no hard-block affinity to respect, the placer will beat your intuition and a pblock will only get in its way. Floorplan when there is a reason — an SLR boundary to respect, a hard block to sit next to, a repeating structure to align, or a proven congestion hotspot. "The design is big" is not a reason.

Q: phys_opt_design did nothing. Is it broken?

A: It has a narrow remit: it makes physical optimisations to paths that are already close — replicating drivers, retiming across placed registers, rewiring equivalent outputs. If your worst path is failing by 800 ps with 11 levels of logic, there is nothing physical to optimise and it will correctly report no improvement. Its sweet spot is the last 50–150 ps. Try -directive AggressiveExplore when you are in that range, and something else when you are not.

Q: What is the Rent exponent in report_design_analysis -complexity, in practical terms?

A: A measure of how interconnected a region's netlist is — how many external connections a block of logic needs, as a function of its size. A high value means the logic is intrinsically hard to partition, so no placement can make its wires short. Practically: a high Rent exponent tells you the congestion is coming from your architecture (a crossbar, a full mesh, a wide shared bus) and that placement tuning will not help. It is the number that tells you to stop tuning and go change the RTL.

Q: Can I just let the router run longer?

A: Routing effort is controlled by directives rather than by time, and -directive Explore or AggressiveExplore genuinely do search harder. But if the router is failing because demand exceeds supply in a region, more effort finds more detours, not a solution — and detours cost timing. A router that runs for six hours and succeeds has usually produced a design whose timing is worse than one that routed in forty minutes.

Q: How do I stop the placer scattering my module across the device?

A: First check that it is actually scattered rather than that you assume it is — highlight_objects [get_cells -hier -filter {NAME =~ "*u_mod*"}] in the Device view answers it in seconds. If it is, the cause is usually that something in the module is tied to a distant resource (an I/O, a hard block, a clock), and the placer is trading module locality for that connection. Fix the cause, or pblock the module — generously sized — so the trade is made your way.

docs.title: Bullet Points
docs.text:
• Utilisation is a timing parameter. < 70 %: not your problem. 70–85 %: normal. 85–90 %: everything gets slower and noisier. > 90 %: you are buying closure with engineering weeks.
  • Congestion levels run 1–8. Level 5 is the threshold for action. Below it, work on timing; at or above it, congestion is your timing problem.
  • Local congestion at low overall utilisation means a local cause: high fanout, a hard-block hotspot, a high Rent-exponent structure, or a too-tight pblock.
  • Size pblocks for ≤ 70 % internal utilisation. A pblock at 95 % manufactures the congestion it was meant to prevent. Room inside is not waste.
  • Leave CONTAIN_ROUTING false unless you have proven you need it, and align pblocks to CLOCKREGION boundaries.
  • Fanout before floorplan. report_high_fanout_nets then MAX_FANOUT or RTL replication is cheaper and more effective than a pblock.
  • [Place 30-574] is a hardware finding, not a constraint request. Fix the pin if you can; if you cannot, apply CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE FALSE, measure the skew, and file a board change.
  • Congestion directives: place_design -directive AltSpreadLogic_high / SSI_SpreadLogic_high, phys_opt_design -directive AggressiveExplore, route_design -directive AlternateCLBRouting.
  • Reports: report_design_analysis -congestion -complexity, report_high_fanout_nets -timing -load_types, report_utilization -pblocks, report_clock_networks.

docs.title: Section 4.3: Design Closure and Iteration: The Final Polish
docs.text:
You’ve synthesized your design, placed it on the grid, and routed the wires. Now comes the most intense part of the FPGA lifecycle: Timing Closure. This is the process of ensuring that every single signal in your design reaches its destination before the next clock edge. If even one signal is a few picoseconds late, your design is officially "broken."

In the AMD UltraFast Methodology, design closure is not a one-time event; it’s an iterative loop. You run the tools, analyze the results, tweak your code or constraints, and run them again. It’s the final polish that turns a "good" design into a "production-ready" one.

docs.title: The Final Polish: Reaching the Finish Line
docs.text:
When you run the implementation tools, Vivado generates a Timing Report. This report is your roadmap for closure. It tells you the "Worst Negative Slack" (WNS)—the amount of time by which your slowest path failed. If WNS is positive, you’ve met timing. If it’s negative, you have work to do.

Think of timing closure like a professional athlete trying to shave a fraction of a second off their personal best. You aren't looking for massive changes anymore; you’re looking for tiny optimizations—a LUT here, a register there—that will give you the slack you need to cross the finish line.

Brain Power If your design fails timing by 50 picoseconds, should you go back and rewrite the entire RTL? Or should you try different implementation strategies first? What is the "Rule of Diminishing Returns" in timing closure?

docs.title: Slack Analysis: The Margin of Safety
docs.text:
Slack is the difference between the "Required Time" (when the signal must arrive) and the "Arrival Time" (when the signal actually arrives). Positive slack is your margin of safety. Negative slack is a timing violation.

Analyzing slack is about finding the "Low-Hanging Fruit." Sometimes a path fails because of a single long wire. Other times, it fails because of a massive chain of logic. By identifying the reason for the negative slack, you can choose the right tool to fix it. If the delay is mostly logic, pipeline it. If the delay is mostly routing, try a different placement strategy.

docs.title: Fireside Chat: The Perfectionist and the Practical Engineer
docs.text:
Perfectionist: "I’ve been iterating on this 10G Ethernet core for three days. I’ve reached 10 picoseconds of positive slack, but I want to get it to 100. I’m going to try one more implementation strategy."

Practical Engineer: "Why? 10 picoseconds of positive slack is a pass. The bitstream will work. The hardware doesn't care if you passed by a mile or an inch. We need to ship this product by Friday."

Perfectionist: "But what if the temperature changes? What if the voltage drops? 10 picoseconds feels too risky!"

Practical Engineer: "Vivado’s timing analysis already accounts for 'Worst Case' temperature and voltage. If the tool says you passed, you passed. Stop chasing ghosts and start working on the user manual. Done is better than perfect."

docs.title: The Timing Report Deep Dive: The Autopsy
docs.text:
When a path fails timing, you need to perform an "Autopsy." The Timing Summary report shows you the exact breakdown of the delay. It tells you how much time was spent in the LUTs, how much in the flip-flops, and how much in the copper wires.

Look for the Logic Levels. If a path has 15 levels of logic between registers, it will never meet timing at 400MHz. You need to "break" that path by adding registers (Pipelining). If the report shows a single "Route Delay" that is 80% of the total path, you have a placement problem. Implementation can move logic and reroute nets; it cannot restructure your RTL. Use the autopsy to find the root cause.

docs.title: Critical Path Optimization: Shaving Picoseconds
docs.text:
Once you’ve found your critical paths, you have several techniques for optimizing them:

  1. Retiming: Moving registers across logic boundaries to balance the delay.
  2. Logic Replication: Creating multiple copies of a high-fanout signal to reduce the load on a single driver.
  3. Physical Constraints: Using USER_PBLOCKS or LOC constraints to force the tools to place critical components closer together.

These are "surgical" interventions. You don't want to use them on the whole design—just on the few paths that are causing you pain.

docs.title: Code Detective: The False Path Fallacy
docs.text:
Sometimes, a path "fails" timing, but the failure doesn't actually matter. These are called False Paths.

# Code Detective: Why is this 'set_false_path' dangerous?
set_false_path -from [get_pins reset_reg/C] -to [all_registers]
# Hint: Is there any scenario where the timing of the reset signal actually MATTERS?

The flaw here is a "Global False Path" on the reset signal. While the activation of a reset is often asynchronous, the release of a reset must be synchronous to the clock. If some registers come out of reset one cycle before others, your state machine could end up in an illegal state.

Name the checks being deleted, because that is what makes it concrete. Timing analysis of a reset consists of recovery (the reset must deassert far enough before the clock edge, the analogue of setup) and removal (it must stay deasserted far enough after, the analogue of hold). A false path on the reset deletes both. The design then meets timing while containing a reset network that can release different flops on different cycles — and a one-hot state machine that comes out of reset with two bits set is a machine that never reaches a legal state again until the next power cycle.

The fix is to make the release synchronous so the checks pass rather than disappearing:

// Asynchronous assert, synchronous release - one macro, per destination domain.
xpm_cdc_sync_rst #(
    .DEST_SYNC_FF (4),
    .INIT         (1),      // reset asserted at power-up
    .INIT_SYNC_FF (1)
) u_rst_sync (
    .src_rst  (async_rst_in),   // asserts immediately, no clock required
    .dest_clk (clk),
    .dest_rst (rst)             // deasserts synchronously to clk
);

# Now the reset is a normal synchronous signal in each domain, and recovery/removal
# analysis is meaningful. The only exception you need is on the ASYNCHRONOUS INPUT
# to the synchronizer - narrowly scoped, not global:
set_false_path -from [get_ports async_rst_in] -to [get_cells u_rst_sync/*]

# Verify, rather than assume:
report_timing -to [get_cells -hier -filter {NAME =~ "*rst*" && IS_SEQUENTIAL}] \
              -delay_type min_max -max_paths 20
check_timing -verbose        ;# look for missing recovery/removal analysis
report_cdc -details          ;# reset crossings show up here too

The distinction to carry away: narrow, justified exceptions on genuinely asynchronous signals are correct engineering; broad exceptions that make reports look good are self-deception. A set_false_path -to [all_registers] is always the second kind.

docs.title: Analogy → Silicon
docs.text: In the story In the silicon Where the analogy breaks Shaving a fraction off a personal best Recovering the last tens of picoseconds with phys_opt_design and directive sweeps An athlete improves monotonically; implementation results are noisy, and the same design can move ±50 ps between runs on identical inputs The autopsy Decomposing a failing path into \(T_{co}\), logic delay, net delay and Logic Levels An autopsy has one cause of death; a failing path usually has a dominant term and several contributing ones, and the split tells you which Surgery on a critical path MAX_FANOUT, logic replication, LOC/pblock constraints, retiming Surgery is local by nature; a LOC constraint on a busy region displaces other logic and can create a new critical path elsewhere "Done is better than perfect" Sign-off at a positive WNS against a complete constraint set The sentiment is right and the emphasis is wrong: the risk is not insufficient margin, it is an incomplete constraint set that made the margin meaningless Diminishing returns The point where a directive sweep costs more machine-hours than the picoseconds are worth Returns diminish smoothly in the analogy; here there is a step change — an architectural fix restarts the curve, a heuristic does not

docs.title: Decomposing a failing path into an action
docs.text:
The whole skill of closure is turning one report into one decision. The decomposition:

\[T_{\text{path}} = T_{co} + T_{\text{logic}} + T_{\text{net}}\]

Givens — three failing paths from a real timing summary, all on a 2.500 ns clock:

Path Data Path Delay logic route Logic Levels Slack A 2.910 ns 2.331 ns (80 %) 0.579 ns (20 %) 12 −0.431 ns B 2.870 ns 0.574 ns (20 %) 2.296 ns (80 %) 3 −0.391 ns C 2.760 ns 1.380 ns (50 %) 1.380 ns (50 %) 6 −0.281 ns

Path A — logic-dominated, 12 levels. Target the depth. If you split it into two balanced stages:

\[T_{\text{logic,new}} \approx \frac{2.331}{2} = 1.166\ \text{ns} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad T_{\text{path}} \approx 0.089 + 1.166 + 0.579 = 1.834\ \text{ns}\] \[\text{Slack} \approx 2.479 - 1.834 = +0.645\ \text{ns} \quad \checkmark\]

Cost: one cycle of latency. Verdict: pipeline it.

Path B — route-dominated, only 3 levels. Pipelining would split 574 ps of logic and leave 2.296 ns of routing untouched:

\[T_{\text{path,new}} \approx 0.089 + 0.287 + 2.296 = 2.672\ \text{ns} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{Slack} \approx -0.193\ \text{ns}\]

Still failing, and you have paid a cycle of latency for it. Verdict: do not pipeline. Attack the route — check fanout, replicate the driver, pull the endpoints together. If a single net is most of that 2.296 ns, MAX_FANOUT alone may fix it.

Path C — balanced. This is the one where a directive sweep and phys_opt_design are genuinely the right tools, because there is no single dominant term to attack.

The rule extracted: compute the post-fix delay before doing the fix. Two minutes of arithmetic routinely saves a day of implementation runs.

docs.title: When to stop
docs.text:
\[\text{Value of continuing} = \Delta\text{WNS expected} \times \text{probability of success} - \text{engineering cost}\]

Givens — typical numbers, worth calibrating against your own history:

Action Expected ΔWNS Machine cost Engineering cost One more directive +10 to +50 ps 3 h ~0 Full directive sweep (20 runs) +50 to +150 ps 68 h ~0.5 day Fanout / replication fix +100 to +400 ps 3 h 0.5 day Pipeline a critical path +300 to +800 ps 3 h 1–3 days (incl. re-verification) Floorplan a congested region +100 to +500 ps 6 h 1–2 days

If you are at −0.050 ns, a directive sweep is the correct answer and pipelining is absurd. If you are at −0.600 ns, sweeping is a way to spend three days proving you needed to pipeline. Match the tool to the size of the deficit — that single habit is most of what separates a two-day closure from a three-week one.

docs.title: The Real Artifact
docs.text:
An implementation script built around the closure loop, with the incremental flow that makes iteration cheap.

#==============================================================================
# impl.tcl - implementation with a closure loop that converges.
#
# Two features that pay for themselves immediately:
#   * QoR suggestions are written after one run and READ BACK on the next, so the
#     tool acts on its own advice instead of just printing it.
#   * Incremental implementation reuses the previous placement/routing, cutting
#     runtime dramatically for small changes - which is what makes an iterative
#     loop practical rather than a once-a-day ritual.
#==============================================================================

set build ./build
set ref   $build/routed_reference.dcp

open_checkpoint $build/post_synth.dcp

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Reuse the previous run's placement when the change was small.
#    'more_than_pin_swaps' means: reuse aggressively, but re-place anything the
#    netlist change actually affected.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
if {[file exists $ref]} {
    read_checkpoint -incremental $ref
    puts "INFO: incremental flow enabled against $ref"
}

# Feed back what the tool told us last time.
if {[file exists $build/qor.rqs]} {
    read_qor_suggestions $build/qor.rqs
}

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The flow. Directives start at Default and change only in response to a
#    diagnosis - see "Do the Math".
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
opt_design      -directive Default
place_design    -directive Default
phys_opt_design -directive Default
route_design    -directive Default

# The second phys_opt pass, post-route, is frequently worth 30-80 ps and costs
# minutes. Skipping it is leaving free margin on the table.
phys_opt_design -directive AggressiveExplore

write_checkpoint -force $build/post_route.dcp

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Sign-off reports. All of them, every time - a build whose reports you did
#    not generate is a build you cannot reason about later.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
report_timing_summary -delay_type min_max -report_unconstrained \
    -check_timing_verbose -max_paths 10 -file $build/timing_summary.rpt

report_design_analysis -logic_level_distribution \
    -of_timing_paths [get_timing_paths -max_paths 1000 -slack_lesser_than 0] \
    -file $build/logic_levels.rpt

report_qor_suggestions -file $build/qor_suggestions.rpt
write_qor_suggestions -force $build/qor.rqs

report_methodology -file $build/methodology.rpt
report_cdc -details   -file $build/cdc.rpt
report_utilization    -file $build/utilization.rpt

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The gate. Sign-off is not "WNS is positive" - it is "WNS is positive AND
#    the constraint set is complete AND the methodology checks pass."
#    A positive WNS on an incomplete constraint set is a wrong answer, not a
#    lenient one.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
proc signoff_gate {} {
    set wns [get_property SLACK [get_timing_paths -delay_type max -max_paths 1]]
    set whs [get_property SLACK [get_timing_paths -delay_type min -max_paths 1]]

    set fail 0
    if {$wns < 0} { puts "FAIL: WNS = $wns ns";  set fail 1 }
    if {$whs < 0} { puts "FAIL: WHS = $whs ns";  set fail 1 }

    # Unconstrained endpoints mean the tool was never asked about part of your
    # design, and that matters MORE than the WNS number above it. There is no
    # clean Tcl accessor, so read it back out of the summary we just wrote.
    set fh [open $::build/timing_summary.rpt r]
    set summary [read $fh]
    close $fh
    if {[regexp {There are (\d+) register/latch pins with no clock} $summary -> n]} {
        puts "FAIL: $n register/latch pin(s) with no clock - see check_timing section"
        set fail 1
    }

    # Methodology violations that are timing-related are not style advice.
    set meth [get_methodology_violations -quiet -severity {CRITICAL WARNING}]
    if {[llength $meth] > 0} {
        puts "FAIL: [llength $meth] methodology violation(s) - see methodology.rpt"
        set fail 1
    }

    # CDC criticals are functional bugs, and they do not appear in WNS at all.
    set cdc [get_cdc_violations -quiet -severity Critical]
    if {[llength $cdc] > 0} {
        puts "FAIL: [llength $cdc] critical CDC violation(s) - see cdc.rpt"
        set fail 1
    }

    if {$fail} {
        error "Sign-off gate failed."
    }
    puts "SIGN-OFF PASSED: WNS $wns ns, WHS $whs ns, no methodology or CDC criticals."
}

signoff_gate

# Keep this run as the reference for the next incremental iteration.
file copy -force $build/post_route.dcp $ref

docs.title: Sharpen Your Pencil
docs.text:
1. A path has Data Path Delay: 3.400ns (logic 0.680ns (20%) route 2.720ns (80%)), Logic Levels: 2, on a 3.000 ns clock. Compute the slack improvement you would expect from pipelining it, and say what you would do instead.
  2. Your design is at WNS −0.045 ns with TNS −0.045 ns. Using the cost table above, pick your next action and justify it in one sentence.
  3. report_timing_summary shows WNS +0.312 ns, and check_timing reports 47 unconstrained_internal_endpoints. Is this design ready to ship? Explain what the +0.312 ns actually means.

docs.title: Final Thoughts on Closure
docs.text: Timing closure is where the science of FPGA design meets the grit of engineering. It’s about persistence, analysis, and knowing when to stop. By mastering the timing report and learning to perform autopsies on your critical paths, you ensure that your design is robust, reliable, and ready for the real world. Polish the design, close the timing, and claim your victory.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
Brain Power — Failing by 50 ps: rewrite the RTL, or try implementation strategies first? What is the rule of diminishing returns here?

Try implementation strategies. At 50 ps you are inside the range where heuristics operate. From the cost table: one more directive is expected to be worth 10–50 ps at essentially zero engineering cost, and a phys_opt_design -directive AggressiveExplore post-route pass alone frequently finds 30–80 ps. Rewriting RTL for 50 ps means days of work plus re-verification, to buy something a three-hour machine run probably delivers.

The rule of diminishing returns, stated usefully: each successive fix has a smaller expected gain and a larger cost, so match the tool to the size of the deficit.

Deficit Right tool < 50 ps phys_opt_design, one directive change 50–150 ps Directive sweep, fanout reduction 150–400 ps Replication, targeted floorplanning > 400 ps Architecture: pipelining, restructuring, a different device

The critical nuance the analogy misses: the curve is not smooth. An architectural fix does not give you a slightly better result than a directive — it restarts the curve at a new baseline. So "diminishing returns" applies within a class of fix, not across classes. Someone who sweeps directives for a week on a −0.600 ns design is not experiencing diminishing returns; they are using the wrong tool, indefinitely.

One more thing worth saying about the 50 ps case, since the Fireside Chat above touches it: the reason 10 ps of positive slack is genuinely acceptable is not that "the tool accounts for the corners so you passed." It is that sign-off is against your constraint set, at characterised corners, with clock uncertainty already subtracted. The question worth worrying about is therefore never "is 10 ps enough margin?" but "is my constraint set complete?" — which is what Sharpen Your Pencil #3 is about.

Sharpen Your Pencil #1 — 3.400 ns path, route 80 %, Logic Levels: 2, 3.000 ns clock.

Pipelining splits the logic term only:

\[T_{\text{new}} \approx T_{co} + \frac{0.680}{2} + 2.720 = 0.089 + 0.340 + 2.720 = 3.149\ \text{ns}\]

Against a required time of roughly 2.95 ns (period minus setup and uncertainty), that is still about −0.20 ns — still failing, after spending a cycle of latency and a round of re-verification. And note that with only 2 levels of logic there may not even be a sensible place to insert a register.

What to do instead: 2.720 ns of route on a 2-level path means one or two enormous nets. Find them:

report_timing -to <endpoint> -input_pins -max_paths 1
report_high_fanout_nets -timing -load_types -max_nets 25

Then, in order of cost: reduce the fanout (MAX_FANOUT or RTL replication); let phys_opt_design replicate the driver; check whether the path crosses an SLR boundary un-pipelined (Section 1.4 — that alone can be 2 ns); check whether the endpoints are in a congested region (Section 4.2). A 2-level path with 2.7 ns of routing is almost always a structural problem — distance, fanout, or a boundary — not a logic problem.

Sharpen Your Pencil #2 — WNS −0.045 ns, TNS −0.045 ns.

TNS equalling WNS means exactly one failing path, failing by 45 ps.

Action: phys_opt_design -directive AggressiveExplore post-route, then one alternative route_design directive if that is not enough. Justification in one sentence: a single path 45 ps short is precisely the regime where physical optimisation operates, at three hours of machine time and zero engineering time, against a fix whose alternatives all cost days.

What not to do: a full 20-run directive sweep (68 hours to solve a one-path problem), or any RTL change. If two rounds of physical optimisation do not close it, then look at the one path specifically — one path is cheap to examine by hand.

Sharpen Your Pencil #3 — WNS +0.312 ns with 47 unconstrained internal endpoints.

No, it is not ready to ship, and the +0.312 ns is close to meaningless.

What the number actually means: "of the paths I was asked to analyse, the worst had 312 ps of margin." It says nothing whatsoever about the 47 endpoints that were not analysed. Those paths were not optimised for timing either — the placer and router had no requirement to meet on them — so they will have whatever delay fell out, commonly several times worse than your constrained paths.

Worse, the relationship is perverse: removing constraints improves WNS. A design with 47 unconstrained endpoints reports a better number than the same design fully constrained. So the healthy-looking 312 ps is partly a consequence of the defect.

What to do:

  1. Run check_timing -verbose and read the no_clock, unconstrained_internal_endpoints and no_input_delay/no_output_delay sections.
  2. For each, determine why. The usual causes are a clock that was never declared (often one generated in fabric, or one coming from a transceiver), an IP whose XDC failed to apply because a cell name changed, or genuinely dead logic.
  3. Constrain them, or delete them if they are dead.
  4. Re-run. Expect WNS to get worse, and treat that as the constraint set becoming honest rather than as a regression.

The general principle, and it is the most important one in this chapter: timing sign-off is a statement about your constraint set, not about your design. A green report on an incomplete constraint set is a wrong answer delivered confidently, which is the most expensive kind.

docs.title: There Are No Dumb Questions
docs.text:
Q: Is incremental implementation safe, or does it hide problems?

A: It is safe for what it claims: it reuses the previous placement and routing where the netlist is unchanged, and re-implements what changed. What it does not do is give you an independent result — so before sign-off, do one clean, non-incremental run. Use incremental during the closure loop, where its runtime saving is what makes iteration practical, and clean for the build you ship.

Q: Why do I get different results from identical runs?

A: Implementation uses heuristics with multi-threaded, order-dependent internals, so identical inputs can produce results differing by tens of picoseconds. Set the number of threads explicitly (set_param general.maxThreads 8) if you need repeatability. The practical consequence: do not celebrate or panic over a ±30 ps change. If you are tracking whether a fix helped, look at TNS and at the distribution of failing paths, not at WNS alone.

Q: report_qor_suggestions gave me twenty suggestions. Do I apply them all?

A: Read them first — they are ranked and they explain themselves. Some are automatic (written to the .rqs file and consumed by opt_design); others are RTL changes you must make. Apply the automatic ones freely, evaluate the RTL ones on merit. The single most valuable thing in that report is usually its identification of which structural problem dominates, which is diagnosis you would otherwise do by hand.

Q: Can I sign off with methodology warnings outstanding?

A: Some, with justification. But the TIMING-* family in particular are not style advice — they flag situations where the timing analysis itself is unreliable: clocks with no common node, unconstrained crossings, clocks generated by fabric logic, LUTs on clock paths. A methodology warning of that kind means your WNS is describing something other than your design. Treat those as blocking; waive the cosmetic ones with a written reason.

Q: My WNS is positive but the board fails intermittently. Where do I look?

A: In roughly this order: unconstrained paths (check_timing); CDC (report_cdc — CDC failures never appear in WNS at all); reset release and recovery/removal; clock quality and jitter on the board (Sections 1.2 and 1.3); then power integrity under load. Note that the first three are all "the timing report was answering a different question than you thought," which is the theme of this section.

docs.title: Bullet Points
docs.text:
• Decompose before you fix. Compute the post-fix delay from the logic/route split. Pipelining a route-dominated path costs a cycle and closes nothing.
  • Match the tool to the deficit: < 50 ps → phys_opt_design; 50–150 ps → directive sweep, fanout; 150–400 ps → replication, floorplan; > 400 ps → architecture.
  • Diminishing returns applies within a class of fix, not across classes. An architectural change restarts the curve.
  • Run phys_opt_design again after route_design. Typically 30–80 ps for minutes of runtime.
  • Feed the tool its own advice: write_qor_suggestions → read_qor_suggestions on the next run. Use read_checkpoint -incremental to make the loop fast.
  • A false path on a reset deletes recovery and removal analysis. Use xpm_cdc_sync_rst for synchronous release, and scope the exception to the asynchronous input only.
  • Sign-off is WNS ≥ 0 AND WHS ≥ 0 AND a complete constraint set AND no methodology or CDC criticals. Removing constraints improves WNS, so a green report on an incomplete constraint set is a wrong answer.
  • Expect ±30 ps of run-to-run noise. Track TNS and the failing-path distribution, not WNS alone.
  • Reports: report_timing_summary -check_timing_verbose -report_unconstrained, report_design_analysis -logic_level_distribution, report_qor_suggestions, report_methodology, report_cdc -details.

docs.title: Section 5.1: Power Estimation and Optimization: The Energy Budget
docs.text:
In the early days of FPGAs, power was an afterthought. But as chips have gotten smaller and faster, they’ve also gotten hungrier. Today, Power Management is a first-class citizen in the AMD UltraFast Methodology. If your FPGA consumes too much power, it will get too hot, its performance will degrade, and it might even melt the solder off your board.

Think of your FPGA as a high-performance sports car. If you drive it at 200mph all day, you're going to burn a lot of fuel and generate a lot of heat. Power estimation is your "Fuel Gauge," and optimization is your "Fuel Efficiency" package.

docs.title: The Energy Budget: Static vs. Dynamic Power
docs.text:
Power consumption in an FPGA comes in two flavors:

  1. Static Power (Leakage): This is the power the chip consumes just by being turned on. Even if no logic is switching, electrons are "leaking" through the transistors. Static power is mostly a function of the chip’s size and temperature.
  2. Dynamic Power: This is the power consumed when your logic signals toggle from 0 to 1. Every time a wire changes state, it charges and discharges tiny capacitors, which consumes energy. Dynamic power is a function of your clock frequency and how much logic is active.

Managing your energy budget means attacking both types of power. You can't do much about static power (other than keeping the chip cool), but you have total control over dynamic power.

Brain Power If you double the clock frequency of your design, does the dynamic power consumption double, quadruple, or stay the same? Why does reducing the voltage have a much larger impact on power than reducing the frequency?

docs.title: XPE: The Financial Planner for Power
docs.text:
AMD provides a powerful tool called the Xilinx Power Estimator (XPE). It’s a sophisticated spreadsheet that allows you to predict your power consumption before you even write a single line of code.

Think of XPE as your "Financial Planner." You tell it which FPGA you’re using, your expected clock frequencies, and how many LUTs and DSPs you plan to use. XPE then gives you a detailed breakdown of your power needs. This allows you to design your Power Delivery Network (PDN) and your cooling system before the hardware is built. Don't build a board without an XPE report; it’s like going on a shopping spree without checking your bank balance.

docs.title: Fireside Chat: The Performance Junkie and the Green Engineer
docs.text:
Performance Junkie: "I’ve got the DSP engine running at 600MHz! The data throughput is incredible! We’re going to crush the competition."

Green Engineer: "That’s great, but the chip is pulling 50 Watts and the heatsink is glowing red. We’re going to kill the battery in twenty minutes, and the fan is so loud it sounds like a jet engine."

Performance Junkie: "So what? Speed is everything!"

Green Engineer: "Not if the chip shuts down due to over-temperature. I can use 'Clock Gating' to turn off the DSP blocks when they aren't processing data. We’ll keep 90% of the performance but cut the power consumption in half. Efficiency is the ultimate performance hack."

docs.title: Clock Gating: Turning Off the Lights
docs.text:
The most effective way to save dynamic power is Clock Gating. This means disabling the clock signal to parts of your design that aren't currently being used. If the clock doesn't toggle, the flip-flops don't toggle, and the dynamic power drops to zero.

Vivado can perform some clock gating automatically, but for the best results, you should design it into your RTL. Use "Clock Enables" (CE) on your registers. When CE is low, the register stays silent. It’s like turning off the lights in a room when you leave—it’s a simple habit that saves a ton of money (and heat).

docs.title: Voltage Scaling: The Lean Diet
docs.text:
AMD FPGAs often support multiple voltage levels for their internal logic. By running your chip at a slightly lower voltage (e.g., 0.72V instead of 0.85V), you can drastically reduce power consumption. This is because power is proportional to the square of the voltage (\(P \propto V^2\)).

However, lower voltage also means slower transistors. You have to balance your desire for low power with your need for high speed. The UltraFast methodology recommends using the "VCCINT_IO" and "VCCINT" scaling features wisely to find the "Sweet Spot" for your specific application.

docs.title: Code Detective: The Glitchy Logic Power Drain
docs.text:
Combinational "Glitches" can be a silent power killer. A glitch is when a logic signal toggles multiple times before settling on its final value.

// Code Detective: Why will this logic consume unnecessary power?
assign out = (a & b) | (c & d) | (e & f);
// Hint: If a, b, c, d, e, and f all change at slightly different times, how many times will 'out' toggle?

The flaw here is a combinational "SOP" (Sum of Products) tree whose inputs arrive at different times. Each arrival can flip the output before it settles, and every one of those extra transitions charges and discharges real capacitance.

Put a number on it, because the effect compounds through a logic cone. If the six inputs arrive at six different times, the output can transition up to six times per evaluation instead of once — and each downstream stage sees those glitches as its input activity, multiplying them again. In a deep unregistered arithmetic tree, glitch power routinely exceeds useful switching power.

The fix — and the more important second half of it:

// Fix 1: register the output. The flop samples once per clock edge, so the
// glitches never leave this stage. Cost: one cycle of latency, one flop.
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    out <= (a & b) | (c & d) | (e & f);
end

// Fix 2 (the one people miss): balance the arrival times. Registering the OUTPUT
// stops glitches propagating onward, but the tree itself still glitches internally,
// and that power is still burned. Registering the INPUTS makes them arrive together,
// which is what actually stops the glitching.
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    a_r <= a;  b_r <= b;  c_r <= c;  d_r <= d;  e_r <= e;  f_r <= f;
    out <= (a_r & b_r) | (c_r & d_r) | (e_r & f_r);
end

Then measure rather than assume, because glitch power is exactly the component that estimation tools get wrong without activity data:

# report_power's default toggle assumptions cannot see glitching. A SAIF from
# gate-level simulation can, because it records actual transition counts.
read_saif  -strip_path tb_top/dut ./sim/post_route.saif
report_power -file power_saif.rpt

# Check the confidence level at the top of the report. "Low" means the tool is
# guessing at toggle rates and the number below it is not an engineering figure.

docs.title: Analogy → Silicon
docs.text: In the story In the silicon Where the analogy breaks Fuel gauge XPE at planning time; report_power on the routed design A fuel gauge measures; both of these estimate, and their accuracy depends entirely on the activity data you feed them — hence the SAIF flow Turning off the lights Clock enables (CE) and BUFGCE gating Lights go fully off; a gated flop still leaks, and the clock tree upstream of the gate still toggles — you save the leaf, not the trunk A lean diet Voltage scaling (\(P \propto V^2\)) Dieting is gradual and reversible; lowering \(V_{CCINT}\) slows transistors, so it is a joint power/timing decision, and it makes your PDN target impedance harder (Section 1.2) Sports car at 200 mph Dynamic power \(\propto \alpha C V^2 f\) A car burns fuel proportional to speed; dynamic power is proportional to toggling, so a fast clock feeding idle logic costs far less than the frequency alone suggests The financial planner XPE's per-resource breakdown A planner works from known income; XPE works from your estimates of resource counts and toggle rates, so its output is only as good as those guesses

docs.title: The one equation, and what each term is worth
docs.text:
\[P_{\text{dynamic}} = \alpha \, C \, V^2 f\]

where \(\alpha\) is the activity factor (fraction of clock cycles on which a node toggles), \(C\) the switched capacitance, \(V\) the supply voltage and \(f\) the clock frequency.

Each term is a different lever with a different exponent, and that is the whole story:

Lever Effect on power Effect on the design \(f\) ÷ 2 linear — halves dynamic power Halves throughput. Usually unacceptable. \(\alpha\) ÷ 2 (clock enables) linear — halves dynamic power in the gated logic Costs a control signal. Usually free. \(C\) ÷ 2 (less logic, shorter nets) linear Requires design work. \(V\) ÷ 2 quadratic — quarters dynamic power Transistors get slower; often not available at all.

Worked example. Take a datapath and compute the saving from clock enables.

Givens:

Symbol Meaning Value \(P_{\text{dyn}}\) Dynamic power of the DSP datapath, always-on 12.0 W Duty Fraction of cycles the datapath has valid data 30 % \(P_{\text{clock tree}}\) Portion of that which is the clock network itself 3.5 W

Gating the data registers with a CE reduces \(\alpha\) on the logic but leaves the clock tree toggling:

\[P_{\text{new}} = \underbrace{3.5}_{\text{clock tree, unchanged}} + \underbrace{(12.0 - 3.5) \times 0.30}_{\text{logic, now gated}} = 3.5 + 2.55 = 6.05\ \text{W}\] \[\text{Saving} = 12.0 - 6.05 = 5.95\ \text{W} \quad (50\ \%)\]

Now gate the clock as well, using BUFGCE so the tree itself stops:

\[P_{\text{new}} = (3.5 + 8.5) \times 0.30 = 12.0 \times 0.30 = 3.6\ \text{W}\] \[\text{Saving} = 8.4\ \text{W} \quad (70\ \%)\]

Verdict: register enables get you half of the available saving; the other half is in the clock tree, and it needs BUFGCE, not CE. That distinction — leaf versus trunk — is the one most power reviews miss.

docs.title: Why voltage scaling is so tempting and so constrained
docs.text:
\[\frac{P_{0.72}}{P_{0.85}} = \left(\frac{0.72}{0.85}\right)^2 = 0.72\]

A 15 % voltage reduction gives a 28 % dynamic power reduction — better than any other single lever. The catch is that transistor delay rises as voltage falls, so your \(F_{max}\) drops, and (from Section 1.2) your PDN target impedance:

\[Z_{\text{target}} = \frac{V \times \text{ripple}}{\Delta I}\]

gets harder on both terms. Voltage scaling is a system decision made at board design time, not a knob you turn during closure.

docs.title: Static power, and why it is a thermal problem
docs.text: Static (leakage) power rises steeply with junction temperature, which raises temperature further, which raises leakage — a positive feedback loop called thermal runaway in its extreme form. Practically: your leakage figure at 100 °C can be several times its 25 °C value, so you cannot compute a power budget without also computing a thermal solution, and vice versa. That is why this section and the next are a pair, and why report_power asks you for a junction temperature.

docs.title: The Real Artifact
docs.text:
The power flow, in the order that actually produces trustworthy numbers, plus the RTL pattern for the clock gating computed above.

#==============================================================================
# power_flow.tcl - from a guess to an engineering number.
#
# The single most common mistake in FPGA power work: quoting report_power's
# default output as if it were a measurement. Its default toggle rate is an
# assumption (typically 12.5% on data nets). Feed it real activity or say
# "estimate" out loud.
#==============================================================================

open_checkpoint ./build/post_route.dcp

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The default estimate. Fast, and its CONFIDENCE LEVEL is the point - check it.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
report_power -file ./build/power_default.rpt
# Read the "Confidence Level" table at the top:
#   Low    - the tool is guessing at toggle rates. Do not quote this number.
#   Medium - some activity data, or a well-characterised design.
#   High   - vectorless with good constraints, or SAIF-driven.

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The real number. Requires a simulation that exercises a representative
#    workload - not a reset test, not a corner case: the thing the product does.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#   In simulation:
#     open_saif ./sim/post_route.saif
#     log_saif  [get_objects -r /tb_top/dut/*]
#     run 100us
#     close_saif
#
read_saif -strip_path tb_top/dut ./sim/post_route.saif
report_power -file ./build/power_saif.rpt

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Where is it going? The per-hierarchy breakdown tells you where to spend
#    effort, and it is almost never where people assume.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
report_power -hierarchical_depth 3 -file ./build/power_hier.rpt

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. What does the tool suggest? This names specific nets and specific fixes.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
report_power_opt   -file ./build/power_opt.rpt
power_opt_design                      ;# automatic clock gating insertion

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Thermal cross-check - power and temperature are one problem (Section 5.2).
#    Set the operating conditions you will actually ship into, not the defaults.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
set_operating_conditions -ambient_temp 55.0 -airflow 250 -heatsink medium
report_power -file ./build/power_hot.rpt
# Compare the static power line against power_saif.rpt. If leakage moved
# significantly, your thermal solution is part of your power budget.

// clock_gate.sv - the trunk, not just the leaf.
//
// Register enables (CE) stop the FLOPS toggling. BUFGCE stops the CLOCK TREE
// toggling as well, which the arithmetic above showed is the other half of the
// available saving.
//
// The critical requirement: BUFGCE's enable is sampled internally to guarantee
// a glitch-free output, but the ENABLE ITSELF must be stable and synchronous to
// the clock being gated. A combinational enable produces a runt clock pulse,
// which is a hardware fault, not a timing violation - it will not show up in
// report_timing.

module gated_datapath (
    input  logic        clk,            // ungated source
    input  logic        rst_n,
    input  logic        work_available, // synchronous to clk
    input  logic [31:0] din,
    output logic [31:0] dout
);

    logic clk_gated;
    logic gate_en;

    // Register the enable so BUFGCE never sees a combinational signal.
    // Extend it by a few cycles so the pipeline drains before the clock stops -
    // stopping the clock with data in flight is a classic source of lost beats.
    localparam int DRAIN = 8;
    logic [DRAIN-1:0] drain_sr;

    always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
        if (!rst_n) begin
            drain_sr <= '0;
            gate_en  <= 1'b0;
        end else begin
            drain_sr <= {drain_sr[DRAIN-2:0], work_available};
            gate_en  <= work_available | (|drain_sr);
        end
    end

    BUFGCE u_gate (.I(clk), .CE(gate_en), .O(clk_gated));

    // Everything below is clocked by the gated clock and costs nothing when idle.
    // NOTE: this creates a new clock. Constrain it - Vivado derives a generated
    // clock at the BUFGCE output, but check the name with report_clocks and make
    // sure any crossing between clk and clk_gated is handled (Section 2.3).
    always_ff @(posedge clk_gated) begin
        dout <= din + 32'd1;
    end

endmodule

docs.title: Sharpen Your Pencil
docs.text:
1. A module dissipates 8.0 W dynamic, of which 2.2 W is its clock network. It has valid data on 40 % of cycles. Compute the power with (a) register enables only, and (b) a BUFGCE gating the whole domain.
  2. Your report_power output says 31.4 W with Confidence Level "Low". Your thermal solution is designed for 35 W. Are you safe? What do you do next?
  3. A colleague proposes running the core at 0.72 V instead of 0.85 V to save power. Compute the dynamic power saving, then list two costs from earlier chapters that this decision imposes.

docs.title: Final Thoughts on the Budget
docs.text: Power is the invisible constraint. It dictates your board size, your cooling costs, and your reliability. By using XPE for early estimation, embracing clock gating, and minimizing combinational glitches, you ensure that your design stays within its energy budget. Keep it lean, keep it efficient, and keep it cool.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
Brain Power — Double the clock frequency: does dynamic power double, quadruple, or stay the same? Why does voltage matter more?

It doubles — linearly. From \(P = \alpha C V^2 f\), power is first-order in \(f\):

\[\frac{P_{2f}}{P_f} = \frac{\alpha C V^2 (2f)}{\alpha C V^2 f} = 2\]

Voltage matters more because it appears squared:

\[\frac{P_{V/2}}{P_V} = \frac{(V/2)^2}{V^2} = \frac{1}{4}\]

Halving the voltage quarters the power; halving the frequency only halves it. The physical reason is that \(V\) enters twice — the charge moved onto a node is \(Q = CV\), and the energy to move it through a potential difference \(V\) is \(QV = CV^2\).

The practically important corollary, though, is the one that makes this more than trivia: voltage and frequency are coupled. Lower voltage means slower transistors, so you cannot take the \(V^2\) saving and keep your frequency. That coupling is why dynamic voltage and frequency scaling reduces energy per operation super-linearly — you drop \(V\) and \(f\) together, giving roughly \(V^3\) — and it is why "just lower the voltage" is a system decision (regulator accuracy, PDN impedance, timing closure at the new corner) rather than a property you set.

Sharpen Your Pencil #1 — 8.0 W total, 2.2 W clock network, 40 % duty.

(a) Register enables only — the logic gates off, the clock tree keeps running:

\[P = \underbrace{2.2}_{\text{clock tree}} + \underbrace{(8.0 - 2.2) \times 0.40}_{\text{logic}} = 2.2 + 2.32 = 4.52\ \text{W}\]

Saving: \(8.0 - 4.52 = 3.48\) W, or 44 %.

(b) BUFGCE gating the whole domain — everything stops together:

\[P = 8.0 \times 0.40 = 3.20\ \text{W}\]

Saving: \(4.80\) W, or 60 %.

The extra 1.32 W is the clock tree, and it is 28 % of the original total — worth noticing that on this module the clock network alone is more than a quarter of the dynamic power. That ratio rises with fanout and with how spread out the domain is, which connects straight back to Section 1.3: a clock whose loads span more clock regions than they need to is burning power on every edge, forever, whether or not the design is doing anything.

Sharpen Your Pencil #2 — 31.4 W, Confidence "Low", thermal solution for 35 W.

You do not know whether you are safe, and 31.4 < 35 is not evidence that you are. "Low" confidence means the tool used default toggle-rate assumptions rather than your design's actual activity. The default is a generic assumption; a design with heavy arithmetic and high data activity can exceed it substantially, and one that is mostly idle can fall far below. The error bar is easily ±30 %, which spans your 3.6 W of headroom several times over.

What to do next, in order:

  1. Get a SAIF. Run a gate-level (or fast functional) simulation of a representative workload — the thing the product actually does under load, not a reset test or a corner case — and feed the SAIF to report_power. This is the single step that moves you from an assumption to a number.
  2. Set the real operating conditions. set_operating_conditions -ambient_temp 55.0 (or whatever your chassis actually is) rather than the 25 °C default. Static power rises steeply with junction temperature, so the default understates leakage for any real enclosure.
  3. Check the split. If static power is a large fraction, your problem is thermal (Section 5.2) and reducing toggling will not help much. If dynamic dominates, the clock-gating arithmetic above is where the wins are.
  4. Then re-evaluate the 35 W margin. And note the direction of the feedback: if the thermal solution is marginal, junction temperature rises, leakage rises, power rises. Budget power and cooling together or neither number is trustworthy.

Sharpen Your Pencil #3 — 0.85 V → 0.72 V.

\[\frac{P_{0.72}}{P_{0.85}} = \left(\frac{0.72}{0.85}\right)^2 = (0.847)^2 = 0.718\]

A 28 % reduction in dynamic power — a genuinely large saving, larger than almost any RTL change would deliver.

Two costs from earlier chapters:

  1. PDN design gets substantially harder (Section 1.2). Target impedance is \(Z = V \times \text{ripple} / \Delta I\). The voltage term falls and, because the same power now flows at a lower voltage, the current term rises. In the worked example there, moving from 0.85 V/20 A to 0.72 V/35 A took the budget from 2.55 mΩ to 0.41 mΩ — over 6× harder, meaning more capacitors, more copper, and a tighter regulator sense loop.
  2. Timing closure gets harder (Chapters 2 and 4). Lower voltage means slower transistors, so every path's delay increases and your achievable \(F_{max}\) drops. A design that closed at 400 MHz at 0.85 V may not at 0.72 V, and recovering it costs pipelining, area and engineering weeks — which may well consume more than the 28 % was worth.

A third, if you want it: regulator accuracy. At 0.72 V a ±3 % tolerance is ±22 mV, and the device's minimum operating voltage does not scale with your ambition. The sense-point placement on the board stops being a detail.

The honest summary for a design review: voltage scaling is the most powerful lever and the one with the most system-level consequences. It is a board-design decision, made early, with the PDN and the timing closure plan on the table.

docs.title: There Are No Dumb Questions
docs.text:
Q: Where does the default toggle rate come from, and can I change it?

A: Vivado applies default switching activity to nets it has no data for, and you can set it explicitly with set_switching_activity — per net, per hierarchy, or by type (-type register, -type lut). Setting it thoughtfully for the parts of your design you understand well is a reasonable middle path between "accept the default" and "produce a full SAIF." What is not reasonable is quoting the default output as a measurement.

Q: Is power_opt_design safe to run?

A: Yes — it inserts clock gating that is functionally transparent (the flops it gates were not going to change value on those cycles anyway). It costs some runtime and can cost a little timing margin on the gated paths. The usual reason not to run it is that you have already done better clock gating by hand at the architectural level, where you can gate whole domains rather than individual registers.

Q: Does an unused portion of the FPGA consume power?

A: Static leakage, yes — a large device leaks more than a small one, irrespective of how much of it you use, and that is a genuine argument for right-sizing the device. Dynamic power, no: unconfigured fabric does not toggle. This is also why bitstream compression helps configuration time in proportion to how empty the device is, and why an oversized device costs you at idle rather than under load.

Q: My design gets slower when it gets hot. Is that a power problem or a timing problem?

A: Both, and they are the same problem viewed from two ends. Higher junction temperature raises leakage (power) and slows transistors (timing), and the tool accounts for the timing side by analysing at the slow/hot corner. What the tool cannot account for is a cooling solution that lets the device run hotter than the corner it was signed off at — so the answer is to make sure your set_operating_conditions and your thermal design agree with each other, which is exactly Section 5.2.

Q: How much power do the transceivers use?

A: Enough that they belong in the budget explicitly rather than as an afterthought — GTs consume power per active lane largely independent of your fabric activity, and a design with many lanes can find that transceivers dominate. report_power's per-block breakdown lists them separately; check that line before optimising fabric toggling.

docs.title: Bullet Points
docs.text:
• \(P_{\text{dynamic}} = \alpha C V^2 f\). Frequency and activity are linear levers; voltage is quadratic. Voltage and frequency are coupled, so you rarely get \(V^2\) for free.
  • Clock enables save the leaf; BUFGCE saves the trunk. In the worked example, CE alone captured 50 % of the available saving and gating the clock tree captured 70 %.
  • A gated clock is a new clock. Constrain it, name it, and handle crossings to the ungated domain.
  • Gate with a registered enable, and drain the pipeline first. A combinational enable into BUFGCE risks a runt pulse, which report_timing will not show you.
  • report_power without activity data is an assumption. Check the Confidence Level before quoting any number. Feed it a SAIF from a representative workload.
  • Set real operating conditions: set_operating_conditions -ambient_temp .... The 25 °C default understates leakage for any real enclosure.
  • Power and thermal are one problem. Leakage rises with junction temperature, which depends on power. Budget both or neither is trustworthy.
  • Register your inputs, not just your outputs, to stop glitch power at the source.
  • Commands: report_power, report_power -hierarchical_depth, report_power_opt, power_opt_design, read_saif, set_switching_activity, set_operating_conditions.
