docs.title: Section 5.2: Thermal Design and Cooling: The Heat Sink Hero
docs.text:
You’ve optimized your power, but you can’t eliminate it entirely. Every watt of power consumed by your FPGA is converted directly into heat. If that heat isn't removed, the internal temperature of the chip will rise until it reaches the Thermal Shutdown limit. At that point, the chip will turn itself off to prevent permanent damage. If you're lucky, it just restarts. If you're unlucky, the thermal stress causes a "latch-up" that destroys the silicon.

In the AMD UltraFast Methodology, thermal design is about managing the journey of heat from the tiny transistors (the Junction) to the outside air. It’s a race against physics, and your primary weapon is the Heat Sink Hero.

docs.title: Junction Temperature (Tj): The Danger Zone
docs.text:
The most important number in your thermal design is the Junction Temperature (\(T_j\)). This is the temperature of the actual silicon inside the package. Most AMD FPGAs have a maximum \(T_j\) of 85°C (Commercial) or 100°C (Industrial).

Think of \(T_j\) as your chip's "Internal Fever." If the fever gets too high, the chip starts acting erratically. Timing paths fail, bits flip randomly, and eventually, the whole system crashes. Your cooling system’s only goal is to keep \(T_j\) comfortably below the limit, even on the hottest day of the year.

Brain Power If the air inside your chassis is 40°C, and your heat sink keeps the chip at 60°C, what is your 'Thermal Margin'? Why does this margin shrink as the FPGA utilization increases?

docs.title: Thermal Resistance: The Traffic Jam for Heat
docs.text:
Heat doesn't just "disappear." it has to flow through multiple layers of material: the silicon, the package, the thermal paste, and finally the heat sink. Each of these materials has a Thermal Resistance (\(\theta\)), measured in °C per Watt.

Think of thermal resistance like a traffic jam on the way to the airport. If the resistance is high, the heat gets backed up inside the chip, and \(T_j\) skyrockets. To keep the chip cool, you need to minimize the resistance at every step. This means using high-quality thermal interface material (TIM) and a heat sink with plenty of surface area.

docs.title: Fireside Chat: The Fan and the Heatsink
docs.text:
Heatsink: "I’m the heavy lifter. I’ve got twenty fins and a massive copper base. I can absorb ten watts of heat without even breaking a sweat. I’m the foundation of this system."

Fan: "That’s cute, but without me, you’re just a hot piece of metal. You can absorb heat, but you can't get rid of it. The air around your fins gets hot and stays there. I’m the one who brings in the fresh, cool air and carries the heat away."

Heatsink: "I don't like moving parts. They're noisy and they fail. I’d rather just be bigger."

Fan: "You don't have the room to be bigger! The chassis is tiny. If you want this FPGA to survive, you need my airflow. Together, we’re a 'Thermal Solution.' Separately, we’re just a future service call."

docs.title: Cooling Strategies: Passive vs. Active
docs.text:
There are two main ways to keep an FPGA cool:

  1. Passive Cooling: Using a heatsink and natural convection (no fan). This is quiet and reliable, but it only works for low-power designs.
  2. Active Cooling: Using a fan to force air across the heatsink. This can handle much higher power but adds noise and a potential point of failure.

In some extreme cases (like high-end Alveo cards used in data centers), even a fan isn't enough. You might need Liquid Cooling, where a special fluid carries the heat away to a remote radiator. Choose the strategy that fits your power budget and your environment.

docs.title: Thermal Monitoring: The SysMon
docs.text:
How do you know if your cooling system is working? You use the SysMon (System Monitor). This is a dedicated piece of hardware inside the FPGA that includes a temperature sensor.

You can read the SysMon through JTAG or through your own HDL logic. The UltraFast methodology recommends setting up Thermal Alarms. If the chip reaches 75°C, have your logic send a warning. If it reaches 85°C, have it go into a low-power "Sleep Mode" or shut down entirely. Don't fly blind—watch the SysMon and stay out of the danger zone.

docs.title: Code Detective: The Sleep Mode logic
docs.text:
You can use the SysMon's OT (Over-Temperature) output to trigger a safety shutdown in your code.

// Code Detective: Why is this shutdown logic dangerous?
always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (sysmon_ot) begin
        logic_reset <= 1'b1; // Stop all switching to save power
    end else begin
        logic_reset <= 1'b0;
    end
end
// Hint: What happens if the clock itself is what's generating the heat?

The flaw here is that the shutdown logic depends on the system clock. If the FPGA is so hot that the clock distribution network is failing, this always block will never execute.

There is a second flaw that bites far more often than the first: this logic holds logic_reset high only while sysmon_ot is high. As soon as the die cools by a fraction of a degree, the reset releases, the design starts switching again, the die heats up, and you get thermal oscillation — a system that alternately runs and resets, forever, at whatever frequency the thermal mass dictates. No hysteresis, no latch.

The fix has three parts, and the third is the one that keeps the board alive:

// Corrected: latched, hysteretic, and with a path that does not need the fabric.
module thermal_guard (
    input  logic clk,
    input  logic rst_n,
    input  logic sysmon_ot,        // hard-block over-temperature, asynchronous
    input  logic sysmon_alm_temp,  // hard-block user-temperature alarm
    input  logic clear_fault,      // explicit software clear - NOT automatic
    output logic throttle,         // reduces activity: gate clocks, drop clock rate
    output logic fault_latched     // sticky, readable by software after the event
);

    // 1. LATCH the event. It must survive the die cooling down, or nobody ever
    //    learns why the board reset itself at 3am.
    always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
        if (!rst_n)            fault_latched <= 1'b0;
        else if (sysmon_ot)    fault_latched <= 1'b1;
        else if (clear_fault)  fault_latched <= 1'b0;
    end

    // 2. HYSTERESIS. Throttle on the OT alarm; keep throttling until the die has
    //    fallen back below the (lower) user-temperature threshold. SYSMON's alarm
    //    registers implement this in hardware if you program both limits - which is
    //    why you configure a warning threshold and a critical threshold, not one.
    logic throttling;
    always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
        if (!rst_n)                       throttling <= 1'b0;
        else if (sysmon_ot)               throttling <= 1'b1;
        else if (!sysmon_alm_temp)        throttling <= 1'b0;   // cooled past the LOW limit
    end

    // 3. The path that does not depend on this module running at all.
    //    OT is driven by the hard block. Combine it directly so a wedged fabric,
    //    a stopped clock or a hung state machine cannot mask a real event.
    assign throttle = throttling | sysmon_ot;

endmodule

And the part that is not RTL at all: the device's own last-resort protection does not need your design. SYSMON's OT output can be routed to a package pin and wired to your power sequencer, so the board can remove power without the FPGA's cooperation. Configure the hard block's shutdown behaviour deliberately:

# Automatic power-down on over-temperature, handled by the hard block itself.
# This is the protection that works when your design is the thing that is broken.
set_property BITSTREAM.CONFIG.OVERTEMPPOWERDOWN ENABLE [current_design]

The principle generalises: a safety mechanism must not depend on the subsystem it is protecting. Throttling in fabric is a good first line; the hard block's own shutdown and a board-level sequencer are the lines that hold when the first one fails.

docs.title: Analogy → Silicon
docs.text: In the story In the silicon / on the board Where the analogy breaks Internal fever Junction temperature \(T_j\), read via SYSMON A fever is a symptom of something else; \(T_j\) is a direct consequence of power and thermal resistance, and it is fully predictable from two numbers Traffic jam for heat Thermal resistance \(\theta\), in °C/W, in series from junction to ambient Traffic clears on its own; thermal resistance is a fixed property of your mechanical design and never improves without a change to it The heatsink hero \(\theta_{SA}\) — the sink-to-ambient resistance you are buying A hero acts; a heatsink is passive, and its rating is meaningless without the airflow it was measured at The fan bringing fresh air Forced convection, which sets \(\theta_{SA}\) Fans are a binary "on"; \(\theta_{SA}\) varies continuously with airflow, and a datasheet figure at 400 LFM is not the figure at 100 LFM inside your chassis Watching the dashboard SYSMON OT and user-temperature alarms with programmed limits A dashboard is informational; these alarms are actuators and must be latched and hysteretic, or they oscillate

docs.title: Do the Math
docs.text:
Thermal design is one equation applied twice — once forwards to predict, once backwards to specify.

\[T_j = T_a + P \times \theta_{JA}\]

and, when you break the path into its series segments:

\[\theta_{JA} = \theta_{JC} + \theta_{CS} + \theta_{SA}\]

(junction-to-case, case-to-sink through the thermal interface material, sink-to-ambient).

docs.title: Forwards: will this survive?
docs.text:
Givens — from report_power, the device datasheet, the TIM datasheet, and your mechanical design:

Symbol Meaning Value \(P\) Total device power (from report_power with a SAIF) 42 W \(T_a\) Worst-case ambient inside the chassis 55 °C \(\theta_{JC}\) Junction-to-case, from the datasheet 0.10 °C/W \(\theta_{CS}\) Case-to-sink, TIM at the specified pressure 0.15 °C/W \(\theta_{SA}\) Heatsink at 200 LFM, from its datasheet 0.55 °C/W \(T_{j,\max}\) Device limit (industrial grade) 100 °C \[\theta_{JA} = 0.10 + 0.15 + 0.55 = 0.80\ \text{°C/W}\] \[T_j = 55 + 42 \times 0.80 = 55 + 33.6 = 88.6\ \text{°C}\] \[\text{Margin} = 100 - 88.6 = 11.4\ \text{°C} \quad \checkmark\]

Passing — but look at where the resistance is. \(\theta_{SA}\) is 0.55 of the 0.80, i.e. 69 % of the total budget is the heatsink and its airflow. That tells you immediately where to spend money if the margin were insufficient, and it tells you that shaving \(\theta_{JC}\) (a device property you cannot change) or fussing over TIM (0.15) has limited upside.

docs.title: Backwards: what must I buy?
docs.text:
This is the calculation that actually belongs in a design review, because it produces a purchasing specification rather than a verdict.

\[\theta_{SA,\max} = \frac{T_{j,\max} - T_a}{P} - \theta_{JC} - \theta_{CS}\]

Same device, but now 60 W and a 45 °C ambient, with a 10 °C design margin held back:

\[\theta_{SA,\max} = \frac{(100 - 10) - 45}{60} - 0.10 - 0.15 = \frac{45}{60} - 0.25 = 0.75 - 0.25 = 0.50\ \text{°C/W}\]

Specification: a heatsink of 0.50 °C/W or better, at the airflow your chassis actually delivers. That last clause is where thermal designs fail — a sink rated 0.50 °C/W at 400 LFM may be 0.90 °C/W at 100 LFM, and your chassis fan curve at the back of a rack in a warm room is not the fan curve on the vendor's test bench.

docs.title: The margin nobody budgets: leakage feedback
docs.text:
Static power rises with \(T_j\), and \(T_j\) rises with power. Take the 42 W case and suppose 15 W of it is leakage, which rises roughly 2 %/°C in this range:

\[\Delta T_j = 33.6\ \text{°C above ambient} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \Delta P_{\text{leak}} \approx 15 \times 0.02 \times 33.6 \approx 10\ \text{W}\]

Feeding that back:

\[T_j = 55 + (42 + 10) \times 0.80 = 55 + 41.6 = 96.6\ \text{°C}\]

Margin collapses from 11.4 °C to 3.4 °C. The first calculation was not wrong so much as incomplete — it used a power figure measured at a temperature the device will not be at. This is why report_power asks for operating conditions, and why the honest flow is to iterate: estimate \(T_j\), re-run report_power at that \(T_j\), recompute.

docs.title: The Real Artifact
docs.text:
A thermal budget you can fill in, and the monitoring that tells you whether reality matched it.

#==============================================================================
# thermal_budget.tcl - compute the specification, then check the design against it.
#
# Run after report_power with a SAIF. The point of doing this in Tcl rather than a
# spreadsheet is that it stays with the design and gets re-run when power changes.
#==============================================================================

# --- Inputs. Replace every one of these with YOUR numbers. --------------------
set P_total     42.0     ;# W    - from report_power (SAIF-driven, at expected Tj)
set T_ambient   55.0     ;# degC - worst case INSIDE the enclosure, not room temp
set T_j_max    100.0     ;# degC - device limit for your temperature grade
set T_margin    10.0     ;# degC - design margin held back
set theta_JC     0.10    ;# degC/W - device datasheet
set theta_CS     0.15    ;# degC/W - TIM at specified pressure and thickness

# --- Backwards: what heatsink do I need? -------------------------------------
set theta_SA_max [expr {($T_j_max - $T_margin - $T_ambient)/$P_total - $theta_JC - $theta_CS}]
puts [format "Required heatsink: <= %.3f degC/W at the airflow your chassis delivers" \
      $theta_SA_max]
if {$theta_SA_max <= 0} {
    puts "IMPOSSIBLE: no heatsink can do this. Reduce power, reduce ambient,"
    puts "  or move to liquid cooling. Do not proceed as if a bigger sink exists."
}

# --- Forwards: what does the sink I actually have give me? -------------------
set theta_SA     0.55    ;# degC/W - the part you can actually buy, at YOUR airflow
set theta_JA [expr {$theta_JC + $theta_CS + $theta_SA}]
set T_j      [expr {$T_ambient + $P_total * $theta_JA}]
puts [format "Predicted Tj = %.1f degC (limit %.1f, margin %.1f)" \
      $T_j $T_j_max [expr {$T_j_max - $T_j}]]

# --- Close the loop: re-run power AT the predicted temperature ---------------
# Leakage is temperature dependent, so the power number that produced this Tj was
# measured at the wrong temperature. Iterate until it converges.
set_operating_conditions -junction_temp $T_j -ambient_temp $T_ambient
report_power -file ./build/power_at_tj.rpt
puts "Re-read the Static Power line in power_at_tj.rpt and repeat if it moved."

#==============================================================================
# sysmon_limits.xdc - the alarm thresholds, and the protection that does not
# depend on your design being alive.
#==============================================================================

# Hard-block automatic power-down on over-temperature. This is the backstop that
# works when the fabric is the thing that has failed. Enable it unless you have a
# specific reason not to.
set_property BITSTREAM.CONFIG.OVERTEMPPOWERDOWN ENABLE [current_design]

# Program TWO thresholds, not one - the gap between them IS the hysteresis:
#   user temperature alarm (upper) : start throttling, log the event
#   user temperature alarm (lower) : stop throttling only after cooling this far
#   OT limit                       : hard-block shutdown
# Generate these INIT words with the System Management Wizard for your device;
# hand-computed alarm registers are a classic "the alarm never fired" bug.
#
# Sanity: the throttle threshold must be BELOW Tj_max minus your margin, or your
# protection engages after the damage rather than before it.

docs.title: Sharpen Your Pencil
docs.text:
1. Your device dissipates 55 W. Chassis ambient is 50 °C, \(T_{j,\max}\) is 100 °C, \(\theta_{JC} = 0.12\) °C/W and \(\theta_{CS} = 0.20\) °C/W. Holding 10 °C of margin, what is the maximum acceptable \(\theta_{SA}\)? Is a 0.6 °C/W sink sufficient?
  2. The same system, but the fan fails and airflow drops from 200 LFM to natural convection, taking \(\theta_{SA}\) from 0.55 to 1.80 °C/W. Compute the new \(T_j\) with 42 W. What must the design do, and how quickly?
  3. Your monitoring shows \(T_j\) stable at 78 °C, well inside limits, and the board still fails intermittently after several hours of operation. Give two thermal explanations that a single junction temperature reading would not reveal.

docs.title: Final Thoughts on the Heat
docs.text: Thermal management is the final boundary of FPGA design. It’s where your digital logic meets the harsh reality of thermodynamics. By understanding junction temperature, minimizing thermal resistance, and monitoring the SysMon, you ensure that your design is not just fast, but also sustainable. Keep it cool, keep it running, and be the heat sink hero your project deserves.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
Brain Power — 40 °C air, heatsink keeps the chip at 60 °C: what is the thermal margin, and why does it shrink as utilisation rises?

First, be careful which temperature "the chip at 60 °C" refers to. If 60 °C is the case temperature, the junction is hotter by \(P \times \theta_{JC}\). Take 42 W and \(\theta_{JC} = 0.10\) °C/W:

\[T_j = 60 + 42 \times 0.10 = 64.2\ \text{°C}\] \[\text{Margin} = T_{j,\max} - T_j = 100 - 64.2 = 35.8\ \text{°C}\]

Comfortable. Now: why does it shrink as utilisation rises? Three mechanisms, and they compound.

  1. Power rises, and margin is linear in power. From \(T_j = T_a + P\theta_{JA}\), every extra watt costs you \(\theta_{JA}\) degrees — here 0.80 °C per watt. Going from 42 W to 60 W costs \(18 \times 0.80 = 14.4\) °C of margin directly.
  2. Leakage rises with temperature, so the extra dynamic power drags static power up behind it. This is the feedback term computed in Do the Math, and it turned an 11.4 °C margin into 3.4 °C in that example.
  3. Hot spots, which the single-number model hides entirely. Utilisation is rarely uniform: a DSP array running at full rate in one clock region can be many degrees above the die average, and SYSMON's sensor reads one location. The average \(T_j\) can look fine while a region is at its limit.

The design conclusion: thermal margin is not a fixed property of the mechanical design. It is a function of the workload, and it must be evaluated at the worst workload you will ship, not at the one that was convenient to simulate.

Sharpen Your Pencil #1 — 55 W, \(T_a = 50\) °C, \(T_{j,\max} = 100\) °C, 10 °C margin.

\[\theta_{SA,\max} = \frac{(T_{j,\max} - T_{\text{margin}}) - T_a}{P} - \theta_{JC} - \theta_{CS}\] \[= \frac{(100 - 10) - 50}{55} - 0.12 - 0.20 = \frac{40}{55} - 0.32 = 0.727 - 0.32 = 0.407\ \text{°C/W}\]

Maximum acceptable \(\theta_{SA}\) is 0.407 °C/W. A 0.6 °C/W sink is not sufficient — check what it would give you:

\[T_j = 50 + 55 \times (0.12 + 0.20 + 0.60) = 50 + 55 \times 0.92 = 50 + 50.6 = 100.6\ \text{°C}\]

That is at the limit with zero margin, before accounting for leakage feedback. You need a better sink, more airflow, lower ambient, or less power — and note that the 10 °C margin you held back is what turned "technically passing" into "clearly failing," which is exactly what design margin is for.

Sharpen Your Pencil #2 — Fan failure, \(\theta_{SA}\): 0.55 → 1.80 °C/W, 42 W.

\[\theta_{JA} = 0.10 + 0.15 + 1.80 = 2.05\ \text{°C/W}\] \[T_j = 55 + 42 \times 2.05 = 55 + 86.1 = 141.1\ \text{°C}\]

141 °C against a 100 °C limit. The device is 41 °C past its rating and heading for permanent damage.

How quickly must the design respond? That depends on thermal mass, and the useful framing is the initial rate of rise. With a package plus heatsink thermal capacitance \(C_{th}\) of roughly 50 J/°C (order of magnitude for a heatsinked BGA), the initial slope after the fan stops is:

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} \approx \frac{P - P_{\text{removed at current }\Delta T}}{C_{th}}\]

Immediately after the failure the sink is still at its old temperature, so the imbalance is small and the rise is gradual — on the order of a degree every few seconds, accelerating. That gives you seconds to a few tens of seconds, not milliseconds, which is genuinely useful: it means a polled software response is fast enough, and you do not need a nanosecond-scale hardware path for this failure.

What the design must do, in layers:

  1. Detect it. The SYSMON user-temperature alarm, with the upper threshold set well below \(T_{j,\max}\) — say 85 °C — so you act on the way up rather than at the limit.
  2. Throttle immediately. Gate clocks (Section 5.1), drop to a reduced clock rate, or halt the highest-power blocks. Cutting power in half roughly halves the temperature rise above ambient: \(T_j = 55 + 21 \times 2.05 = 98\) °C, which is survivable.
  3. Latch and report, so the fan failure is diagnosed rather than experienced repeatedly.
  4. Have the hard-block backstop armed (OVERTEMPPOWERDOWN ENABLE) in case the fabric is not in a position to help.

And note what this exercise really demonstrates: your thermal design has a single point of failure, and it is a moving part. That is worth stating explicitly in a design review, because it is usually the only mechanical failure mode in an otherwise solid-state product.

Sharpen Your Pencil #3 — \(T_j\) stable at 78 °C, board fails intermittently after hours.

Two thermal explanations a single junction reading would not reveal:

  1. A hot spot away from the sensor. SYSMON reads one location on the die. A dense DSP or transceiver region can run substantially hotter than the die average, and a device with multiple SLRs can have a genuinely different temperature per die. The average reads 78 °C while a region sits near its limit — and the failures cluster in the logic that lives there. Larger devices expose more than one sensor; read all of them, and correlate failures with which block is misbehaving rather than with the global number.
  2. A component other than the FPGA. \(T_j\) is the FPGA's junction, not the board's. The DDR4 memory, the voltage regulators, or an HBM stack may be running far hotter than the FPGA, especially if the airflow path puts them downstream of the FPGA's heatsink and they receive pre-heated air. Regulators in particular lose efficiency and accuracy as they heat, so the symptom appears as a rail sagging (Section 1.2) with a perfectly healthy-looking FPGA.

A third, worth mentioning because "after hours" is a clue: thermal cycling and mechanical degradation. TIM pump-out, a loosening heatsink clip, or solder joint fatigue all raise \(\theta\) slowly over time. Failures that appear only after long operation, and that clear on a power cycle, deserve a check of whether \(T_j\) at hour six matches \(T_j\) at minute one — a trend, not a snapshot.

The general lesson: one temperature is one data point. Log \(T_j\) over time, log every sensor the device exposes, and correlate against workload — that is what turns thermal monitoring from a dashboard into a diagnostic.

docs.title: There Are No Dumb Questions
docs.text:
Q: Where do I get \(\theta_{JC}\) and \(\theta_{JA}\)?

A: \(\theta_{JC}\) from the device's package thermal data — it is a property of the silicon and package and you cannot change it. Do not use a datasheet \(\theta_{JA}\) for design: it is measured on a standard test board in still air, which is nothing like your product. Build \(\theta_{JA}\) yourself from \(\theta_{JC} + \theta_{CS} + \theta_{SA}\), where the last term comes from the heatsink vendor at your airflow.

Q: What airflow do I actually have?

A: Less than you think, and it is worth measuring rather than assuming. A chassis fan rated at some CFM delivers that into free air; through a populated board with obstructions, the linear velocity over your heatsink can be a fraction of the nominal figure. If the thermal margin is tight, this is the number most worth measuring on a prototype, because every heatsink specification is conditional on it.

Q: Commercial or industrial temperature grade?

A: Industrial buys you a higher \(T_{j,\max}\) (typically 100 °C versus 85 °C), which is 15 °C of margin — often the difference between needing forced air and not. It costs more per device and it may have different speed grade availability. Decide it during thermal budgeting, because it changes the heatsink specification you compute.

Q: Does the FPGA throttle itself like a CPU does?

A: Not by default and not in the same way. A CPU has an internal DVFS controller; an FPGA does what your design tells it to. The hard block gives you alarms and an optional automatic power-down, but "reduce the clock rate under thermal pressure" is a feature you implement — typically by switching between MMCM outputs with a BUFGCTRL, or by gating clocks as in Section 5.1. If your product needs graceful thermal degradation, design it in.

Q: We are liquid cooled. Is any of this still relevant?

A: All of it, with different numbers. Liquid cooling gives you a much lower \(\theta_{SA}\) equivalent (cold plate to coolant, plus coolant to ambient at the radiator), but the series model, the leakage feedback, and the need for latched hysteretic alarms are unchanged. And you have acquired a new failure mode — pump failure — which behaves like the fan failure above but with less warning, because a cold plate with no flow has very little thermal mass.

docs.title: Bullet Points
docs.text:
• \(T_j = T_a + P \times \theta_{JA}\), and \(\theta_{JA} = \theta_{JC} + \theta_{CS} + \theta_{SA}\).
  • Specify backwards: \(\theta_{SA,\max} = (T_{j,\max} - T_{\text{margin}} - T_a)/P - \theta_{JC} - \theta_{CS}\). That produces a purchasing specification, not an opinion.
  • \(\theta_{SA}\) is usually ~70 % of the budget, so it is where money changes the answer. \(\theta_{JC}\) you cannot change.
  • A heatsink rating without an airflow figure is meaningless. 0.55 °C/W at 400 LFM can be 0.90 °C/W at 100 LFM.
  • Leakage feedback is real: in the worked example it took an 11.4 °C margin down to 3.4 °C. Iterate report_power at the predicted \(T_j\).
  • Use T_a inside the enclosure, not room temperature, and hold back an explicit design margin.
  • Alarms must be latched and hysteretic: two thresholds, not one, or the system oscillates between running and resetting.
  • Safety must not depend on the thing it protects. Arm BITSTREAM.CONFIG.OVERTEMPPOWERDOWN and route OT to the board's sequencer, in addition to any fabric throttling.
  • One temperature is one data point. Log over time, read every sensor, and correlate with workload before concluding the thermals are fine.

docs.title: Section 6.1: Hardware Debugging: The Digital Stethoscope
docs.text:
You’ve simulated your code, you’ve met timing, and you’ve managed the heat. Now comes the moment of truth: you load your bitstream onto the real hardware, and... nothing happens. Or worse, it works for ten minutes and then mysteriously crashes. This is the "Hard Truth" of FPGA design. No matter how much you simulate, there are always bugs that only appear in the real world.

In the AMD UltraFast Methodology, we don't just "guess" what's wrong. we use Hardware Debugging tools to look inside the chip. These tools are your "Digital Stethoscope," allowing you to listen to the heartbeat of your design without even touching a physical probe to the board.

docs.title: The Digital Stethoscope: Peering Inside
docs.text:
Inside every AMD FPGA, there are dedicated resources for debugging. You can "tap" into any internal signal and bring it out to a virtual dashboard on your computer. This means you can see the state of your state machines, the values in your counters, and the handshakes on your AXI buses—all in real-time, while the chip is running at full speed.

Debugging on hardware is a superpower. It allows you to catch the "Ghost Bugs" that only appear when the real world gets messy. But remember: every signal you debug uses a tiny bit of the FPGA's resources. Use your stethoscope wisely.

Brain Power If you add a 1024-sample ILA to a 64-bit bus, how many bits of BRAM are you consuming? If your FPGA is already 95% full, will you still be able to add a large debug core?

docs.title: The ILA: Your High-Speed Waveform Capture
docs.text:
The Integrated Logic Analyzer (ILA) is the workhorse of FPGA debugging. It’s a piece of IP that you drop into your design. It "samples" your signals on every clock edge and stores the data in the FPGA’s internal BRAM. When a specific "Trigger Condition" is met (like an error flag going high), the ILA sends that data back to Vivado, where it’s displayed as a waveform.

Think of the ILA as a high-speed security camera. It’s always watching, but it only "saves" the footage when it sees something suspicious. By setting the right trigger, you can capture the exact moment your logic fails, even if it only happens once every three hours.

docs.title: Fireside Chat: The Lab Tech and the Remote Engineer
docs.text:
Lab Tech: "I’ve been trying to trigger on this 'Packet Error' for two hours. I’ve got the oscilloscope probes hooked up to the output pins, but I can't see what's happening inside the FPGA. I think the bug is in the CRC calculation."

Remote Engineer: "Stop wasting your time with probes. I’ve just instantiated an ILA core on the CRC logic. I’m sitting in my home office, five hundred miles away, and I can see the exact state of the CRC registers on my screen. Look at this... the third bit is flipping incorrectly because of a timing violation."

Lab Tech: "Wait, you can see that from home? Without any probes?"

Remote Engineer: "Yep. JTAG-over-IP. The ILA is my eyes and ears. I don't need to be in the lab to find a logic bug. I just need a network connection and a good trigger condition. Welcome to the future of debugging."

docs.title: The VIO: Pushing Buttons from Your Keyboard
docs.text:
Sometimes you don't need to see high-speed waveforms; you just need to "push a button" or "flip a switch" inside the chip. That’s what the Virtual I/O (VIO) core is for.

The VIO allows you to create virtual buttons and sliders in the Vivado dashboard. You can use them to reset a specific module, change a configuration register, or force an error condition. It’s like having a physical control panel for your FPGA, but it lives entirely on your computer screen. VIOs are great for "Sanity Checking" your design during the first few hours of board bring-up.

docs.title: Debugging Strategies: Finding the Needle
docs.text:
The biggest challenge with hardware debugging is the Data Limit. Because the ILA uses internal BRAM, you can only capture a few thousand samples at a time. If your bug happens over a long period, you’ll never see it in a single capture.

To find the "Needle in the Haystack," you need a clever strategy:

  1. Iterative Triggers: Start with a broad trigger and narrow it down as you learn more.
  2. State Machine Debugging: Bring the 'Current State' signal into the ILA. It’s the single most useful signal for finding logic errors.
  3. Capture Control: Use the "Storage Qualification" feature to only capture data when a specific condition is met (like valid == 1). This allows you to "stretch" your small BRAM buffer across a long period.

docs.title: Code Detective: The ILA Clock Trap
docs.text:
You must connect your ILA core to a clock signal. If you pick the wrong one, your debug data will be garbage.

# Code Detective: Why will this ILA produce confusing results?
# The design has a 400MHz data path and a 10MHz control path.
# The user connects the ILA to the 10MHz clock but probes the 400MHz signals.
# Hint: What happens when you sample a fast signal with a slow clock?

The flaw here is Under-sampling. If you sample a 400MHz signal with a 10MHz clock, you're only seeing one out of every forty transitions.

But under-sampling is the benign half of the problem. The dangerous half is that the ILA is now performing an unsynchronized clock domain crossing on every probe. The 400 MHz signals are asynchronous to the 10 MHz sample clock, so each captured bit can go metastable independently — and a multi-bit bus captured this way tears exactly as described in Section 2.3. The waveform you are shown will contain values that never existed in the design, and you will spend a day debugging them.

The fix:

# Corrected: one ILA per clock domain, each clocked by the domain it probes.

# --- Fast domain ---------------------------------------------------------------
create_debug_core u_ila_400 ila
set_property C_DATA_DEPTH  1024      [get_debug_cores u_ila_400]
set_property C_TRIGIN_EN   false     [get_debug_cores u_ila_400]
set_property C_ADV_TRIGGER true      [get_debug_cores u_ila_400]   ;# multi-state trigger
connect_debug_port u_ila_400/clk [get_nets clk_400]

create_debug_port u_ila_400 probe
set_property PROBE_TYPE DATA_AND_TRIGGER [get_debug_ports u_ila_400/probe0]
set_property PORT_WIDTH 64               [get_debug_ports u_ila_400/probe0]
connect_debug_port u_ila_400/probe0 [get_nets [list {dsp_result[*]}]]

# --- Slow domain ---------------------------------------------------------------
create_debug_core u_ila_10 ila
set_property C_DATA_DEPTH 4096       [get_debug_cores u_ila_10]
connect_debug_port u_ila_10/clk [get_nets clk_10]

# --- Correlate them with cross-triggering rather than a shared clock ------------
# This is what you actually wanted: one domain's event triggering the other's
# capture, WITHOUT sampling one domain's signals on the other's clock.
set_property C_TRIGOUT_EN true [get_debug_cores u_ila_400]
set_property C_TRIGIN_EN  true [get_debug_cores u_ila_10]

If you genuinely need a fast-domain signal visible in a slow-domain capture, cross it properly first — with an xpm_cdc_single or xpm_cdc_handshake — and probe the synchronized version. You lose timing detail, which is honest, instead of gaining fictional values, which is not.

docs.title: Analogy → Silicon
docs.text: In the story In the silicon Where the analogy breaks Digital stethoscope The ILA core: probes, a trigger comparator, and a BRAM capture buffer A stethoscope is passive; an ILA consumes BRAM, LUTs and routing, and inserting one changes the design you are debugging Security camera saving only suspicious footage Trigger conditions plus capture control / storage qualification A camera's storage is effectively unlimited; an ILA's buffer is a handful of BRAMs, and the arithmetic below decides what you can see Virtual control panel The VIO core: fabric-driven inputs and outputs, updated over JTAG Real panel switches are instantaneous; VIO updates are asynchronous to your design and arrive whenever JTAG gets round to it — never use a VIO output as a synchronous control without synchronizing it Watching a race by blinking Sampling one clock domain with another domain's clock Blinking loses information; this fabricates information, because an unsynchronized multi-bit capture shows values that never existed Finding a needle Iterative trigger refinement and multi-state trigger sequences Needles are static; the bug moves as you add probes, because probes change placement, routing and timing

docs.title: What an ILA costs, and therefore what you can afford to see
docs.text:
The capture buffer is real BRAM, and the arithmetic is exact:

\[\text{Storage bits} = \text{probe width (total)} \times \text{capture depth}\] \[\text{BRAMs} = \left\lceil \frac{\text{Storage bits}}{36{,}864} \right\rceil \quad (\text{one RAMB36E2} = 36\ \text{Kb})\]

Givens:

Quantity Value Probes one 64-bit bus, one 32-bit counter, 8 single-bit control signals Capture depth 1024 samples \[W_{\text{total}} = 64 + 32 + 8 = 104\ \text{bits}\] \[\text{Storage} = 104 \times 1024 = 106{,}496\ \text{bits} = 104\ \text{Kb}\] \[\text{BRAMs} = \left\lceil \frac{106{,}496}{36{,}864} \right\rceil = \lceil 2.89 \rceil = 3\ \text{BRAMs}\]

Now the number that changes behaviour. Ask for a deeper window:

Depth Storage BRAMs 1,024 104 Kb 3 8,192 832 Kb 23 32,768 3,328 Kb 91 131,072 13,312 Kb 362

Depth is linear in BRAM, and BRAM is the resource you are most likely to be short of. On a device with 600 BRAMs where your design already uses 480, a 32K-deep capture of 104 bits is affordable and a 128K-deep one is not, regardless of how much you would like it.

docs.title: How long a window is that, really?
docs.text:
\[T_{\text{window}} = \frac{\text{depth}}{f_{\text{sample}}}\]

At 400 MHz:

\[\frac{1024}{400\times10^{6}} = 2.56\ \mu\text{s}\]

2.56 microseconds. If your bug occurs once every three hours, the probability that a blind capture contains it is:

\[\frac{2.56\times10^{-6}}{10{,}800} = 2.4\times10^{-10}\]

Which is the entire argument for triggering: you are not capturing more, you are capturing at the right moment. And it is also the argument for storage qualification — if the interesting events are the 1 % of cycles where valid is high, qualifying the capture on valid stretches the same 1024 samples across 100× more real time:

\[T_{\text{effective}} \approx \frac{1024}{0.01 \times 400\times10^{6}} = 256\ \mu\text{s}\]

Same three BRAMs, a hundred times the coverage.

docs.title: The Real Artifact
docs.text:
The debug flow that keeps the probes out of your RTL, plus a VIO used correctly.

#==============================================================================
# debug.tcl - insert debug on the synthesised netlist, not in the source.
#
# Why not `(* mark_debug *)` in RTL? Because attributes in source get committed,
# forgotten, and shipped. Netlist-based insertion lives in a script you can
# exclude from a production build with one flag.
#
# Usage:
#   synth_design ...
#   source debug.tcl            ;# only when DEBUG_BUILD is set
#   opt_design; place_design; route_design
#==============================================================================

if {![info exists ::env(DEBUG_BUILD)]} {
    puts "INFO: production build - no debug cores inserted."
    return
}

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. An ILA per clock domain. Never share a clock between domains - see the
#    Code Detective above for what that actually does to your waveforms.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
proc add_ila {name clk_net depth probes} {
    create_debug_core $name ila
    set_property C_DATA_DEPTH   $depth [get_debug_cores $name]
    set_property C_TRIGIN_EN    true   [get_debug_cores $name]
    set_property C_TRIGOUT_EN   true   [get_debug_cores $name]
    set_property C_ADV_TRIGGER  true   [get_debug_cores $name]
    set_property C_EN_STRG_QUAL true   [get_debug_cores $name]   ;# capture control
    set_property ALL_PROBE_SAME_MU true [get_debug_cores $name]
    connect_debug_port $name/clk [get_nets $clk_net]

    set idx 0
    foreach {pattern width} $probes {
        if {$idx > 0} { create_debug_port $name probe }
        set port "$name/probe$idx"
        set_property PROBE_TYPE DATA_AND_TRIGGER [get_debug_ports $port]
        set_property PORT_WIDTH $width           [get_debug_ports $port]
        connect_debug_port $port [get_nets [list $pattern]]
        incr idx
    }
}

# The single most useful probe in any design is the state machine's state vector.
# Probe it first, every time. Most "impossible" behaviour is a state machine in a
# state you did not know it could reach.
add_ila u_ila_400 clk_400 1024 {
    {axi_state[*]}      4
    {dsp_result[*]}    64
    {sample_valid}      1
    {fifo_full}         1
    {fifo_empty}        1
}

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Capture control - the technique from "Do the Math" that buys 100x the
#    time window for free. Set the storage qualifier in the hardware manager:
#      set_property CONTROL.CAPTURE_MODE BASIC [get_hw_ilas hw_ila_1]
#      set_property CONTROL.TRIGGER_POSITION 512 [get_hw_ilas hw_ila_1]
#    TRIGGER_POSITION in the middle gives you PRE-trigger history, which is
#    usually where the cause is - the trigger is the symptom.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Keep the probed nets alive through implementation.
#    Without this, opt_design may merge or remove the very net you are probing.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
set_property MARK_DEBUG true [get_nets -hier -filter {NAME =~ "*axi_state*"}]

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Save the probe file. Without it the hardware manager shows probe0, probe1...
#    with no names, and you will spend the session counting bits.
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
write_debug_probes -force ./build/debug_nets.ltx

// vio_control.sv - a VIO used safely.
//
// The trap: VIO outputs change whenever the JTAG chain gets round to updating
// them. They are asynchronous to your fabric clock, and they are NOT glitch free
// across a multi-bit field. Treat every VIO output as an asynchronous input from
// another chip, because functionally that is exactly what it is.

module vio_control (
    input  logic        clk,
    input  logic        rst_n,
    output logic        soft_reset,
    output logic [7:0]  test_mode
);

    logic       vio_reset_async;
    logic [7:0] vio_mode_async;

    vio_0 u_vio (
        .clk        (clk),
        .probe_out0 (vio_reset_async),
        .probe_out1 (vio_mode_async)
    );

    // Single bit: a plain synchronizer is enough.
    xpm_cdc_single #(.DEST_SYNC_FF(3), .SRC_INPUT_REG(0)) u_sync_rst (
        .src_clk (1'b0), .src_in (vio_reset_async),
        .dest_clk(clk),  .dest_out(soft_reset)
    );

    // Multi-bit COHERENT field: independent synchronizers would let it tear,
    // and a torn test_mode is a test mode you never selected. Handshake it.
    xpm_cdc_handshake #(
        .WIDTH(8), .DEST_SYNC_FF(3), .SRC_SYNC_FF(3), .DEST_EXT_HSK(0)
    ) u_sync_mode (
        .src_clk (clk), .src_in (vio_mode_async), .src_send(1'b1), .src_rcv(),
        .dest_clk(clk), .dest_out(test_mode),     .dest_req(), .dest_ack(1'b0)
    );

endmodule

docs.title: Sharpen Your Pencil
docs.text:
1. You want to probe a 256-bit AXI data bus plus 12 control signals at 8,192 samples deep. Compute the storage and the BRAM cost. Your design has 92 BRAMs free. What do you do?
  2. Your bug appears roughly once an hour. Your capture window is 1024 samples at 250 MHz. Compute the window duration and the probability a blind capture catches it. Name the two techniques that change this and say which one to try first.
  3. You add an ILA to investigate a timing-related failure and the failure disappears. Give the two most likely explanations, and say how you would investigate without the ILA.

docs.title: Final Thoughts on the Stethoscope
docs.text: Hardware debugging is where the "Digital Dream" meets the "Physical Reality." It requires patience, logic, and the right tools. By mastering the ILA and the VIO, and by using clever triggering strategies, you can peel back the layers of the silicon and see exactly what your logic is doing. Find the ghosts, fix the bugs, and get your design to the finish line.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
Brain Power — A 1024-sample ILA on a 64-bit bus: how many BRAM bits? And can you add one at 95 % utilisation?

\[\text{Storage} = 64\ \text{bits} \times 1024\ \text{samples} = 65{,}536\ \text{bits} = 64\ \text{Kb}\] \[\text{BRAMs} = \left\lceil \frac{65{,}536}{36{,}864} \right\rceil = \lceil 1.78 \rceil = 2\ \text{RAMB36E2}\]

Two BRAMs — and note the rounding: you asked for 1.78 and you pay for 2. The ILA's own trigger comparators, control logic and JTAG interface cost LUTs and flops on top of that, typically a few hundred of each per core.

At 95 % utilisation, the honest answer is: probably, but not usefully. Two BRAMs may well exist. The problem is everything else:

  • Routing. Probes are nets from wherever the signal lives to wherever the ILA lands. At 95 % utilisation the routing resources to carry 64 bits across the die may simply not be there, and the design will fail to route.
  • Timing. Adding an ILA changes placement, which changes routing, which changes every path in the neighbourhood. At 95 % utilisation a design that closed at +0.020 ns will very likely not close with an ILA in it.
  • The observer effect. If it does close, it closes differently — so you may be debugging a design that no longer exhibits the bug (see Sharpen Your Pencil #3).

What to do instead when the device is nearly full: probe fewer signals (a state vector and two control bits beat a 64-bit bus for most bugs), use a shallower buffer with better triggering, or — the technique people forget — remove functionality temporarily. A build with one processing channel instead of eight has room for instrumentation and usually reproduces the bug.

Sharpen Your Pencil #1 — 256 + 12 = 268 bits, 8,192 deep:

\[\text{Storage} = 268 \times 8192 = 2{,}195{,}456\ \text{bits} = 2{,}144\ \text{Kb}\] \[\text{BRAMs} = \left\lceil \frac{2{,}195{,}456}{36{,}864} \right\rceil = \lceil 59.6 \rceil = 60\ \text{BRAMs}\]

You have 92 free, so it fits — using 65 % of your remaining BRAM on debug.

Whether you should is a different question, and the answer is usually no. What to do instead:

  • Do you need all 256 data bits? For a protocol or state bug, the control signals, the TLAST/TKEEP, and 32 bits of data are almost always enough to find it. Dropping to 44 bits total takes you to 10 BRAMs.
  • Do you need 8,192 samples? With a good trigger, 1,024 usually suffices. Depth compensates for a bad trigger; a good trigger is cheaper.
  • Use storage qualification on TVALID — most AXI-Stream buses are idle most of the time, and qualifying discards the idle cycles for free.

A reasonable final answer: 44 bits × 2,048 samples with capture control ≈ 3 BRAMs, and it will show you more useful cycles than the 60-BRAM version.

Sharpen Your Pencil #2 — 1024 samples at 250 MHz:

\[T_{\text{window}} = \frac{1024}{250\times10^{6}} = 4.096\ \mu\text{s}\] \[P(\text{catch}) = \frac{4.096\times10^{-6}}{3600} = 1.14\times10^{-9}\]

About one in 880 million. You would be capturing for roughly 28 years to expect one hit.

The two techniques:

  1. Triggering. Configure the ILA to arm on the condition that accompanies the failure — an error flag, an unexpected state, a FIFO overflow, a protocol violation. This changes the problem from "sample randomly" to "sample at the moment of interest," and it takes \(P\) from \(10^{-9}\) to 1.
  2. Storage qualification / capture control. Discard uninteresting cycles so the same buffer covers more real time.

Try triggering first, and it is not close. Storage qualification multiplies your window by perhaps 100×, taking \(10^{-9}\) to \(10^{-7}\) — still hopeless. Triggering makes the capture deterministic. Qualification is what you add afterwards, to get more context around a trigger you have already got working.

If you cannot define a trigger — "it just goes wrong eventually" — that is itself the finding: build one. Add an assertion in fabric (a checker that compares against an expected invariant) and trigger the ILA on the assertion firing. That converts an unobservable intermittent bug into a reproducible capture, and it is the single highest-value debug technique in this section.

Sharpen Your Pencil #3 — Adding an ILA makes the failure disappear.

The two most likely explanations:

  1. The insertion changed placement and routing, and the timing-marginal path moved. The ILA displaced logic, the placer rearranged the neighbourhood, and the path that was failing by 20 ps now has 50 ps of slack. The bug is still in the design — it is in a different path now, or it is waiting for the next build to reappear. This is the overwhelmingly common case.
  2. MARK_DEBUG prevented an optimisation that was itself the bug. Probing a net stops it being merged, retimed or absorbed. If the failure depended on that optimisation — say, a net being merged with another that had different timing — preserving it removes the symptom.

How to investigate without the ILA:

  • Static timing analysis, properly. report_timing_summary -check_timing_verbose -report_unconstrained on the non-ILA build. A failure that changes with placement is a timing failure, and STA analyses every path rather than the handful you can probe. Look hardest at what check_timing says is unconstrained.
  • report_cdc -details. Failures that appear and disappear with placement are very often CDC, because routing changes alter the resolution time in the MTBF equation (Section 2.3). CDC failures also never show up in WNS, so a green timing report does not clear them.
  • Build variance as a signal. Implement the design several times with different directives or -seed values. If the failure comes and goes across builds, you have confirmed a marginality rather than a logic bug, and you should stop probing and start fixing margin.
  • Non-invasive observation. Add a counter that increments on the error condition and read it over an existing interface (AXI-Lite register, UART, even a VIO input, which is far cheaper than an ILA). You lose the waveform and keep the design intact — often the right trade for a marginality.

The meta-lesson: when instrumentation changes the behaviour, the instrumentation has told you something. "It disappears when I add an ILA" is not a dead end; it is strong evidence that the bug is timing or CDC marginality rather than logic, and that redirects the whole investigation.

docs.title: There Are No Dumb Questions
docs.text:
Q: MARK_DEBUG in RTL, or create_debug_core in a Tcl script?

A: The script, for anything beyond a quick experiment. RTL attributes get committed and forgotten, and eventually one ships — blocking optimisation in a production build for a debug session someone finished a year ago. Netlist insertion lives in a file you can gate on an environment variable, as in the artifact above. Use RTL attributes when you need to probe a signal that optimisation would otherwise delete before you can reach it.

Q: Why does my ILA show X on some probes?

A: Usually because the net was optimised away and the probe is connected to nothing, or because the design has not come out of reset in that domain. Check the implementation log for messages about debug nets being removed, and confirm the ILA's clock is actually running — an ILA on a gated clock (Section 5.1) captures nothing while the clock is stopped, which looks identical to a dead design.

Q: Can I leave debug cores in a production bitstream?

A: You can, and there are two reasons to think carefully. It costs resources and timing margin permanently. More importantly, it leaves a JTAG-accessible window into your design's internal state, which is a security consideration if you have gone to the trouble of encrypting the bitstream (Section 3.3). Some products deliberately keep a minimal ILA for field diagnosis; that is a decision to make explicitly, not by forgetting to remove it.

Q: What is the single most useful signal to probe?

A: The state vector of whatever state machine governs the failing behaviour. Most "impossible" hardware behaviour resolves to a state machine sitting in a state you did not know it could reach, or cycling between two states because a condition never clears. Probe state first, add data later.

Q: The bug only happens in the field, not on my bench. Now what?

A: Instrument for statistics rather than waveforms. Counters for error events, a minimum/maximum tracker for a FIFO occupancy, a sticky flag for each error class, all readable over an existing management interface. Sticky and cumulative beats a waveform you will never be present to capture — the same argument as the sticky alarms in Sections 1.2 and 5.2. Then use the field data to build a bench reproduction.

docs.title: Bullet Points
docs.text:
• ILA storage \(=\) total probe width × depth. One RAMB36E2 = 36 Kb. Round up.
  • 104 bits × 1024 = 3 BRAMs. 268 bits × 8192 = 60 BRAMs. Depth is linear and expensive.
  • Window duration \(=\) depth \(/ f_{\text{sample}}\). 1024 at 400 MHz is 2.56 µs — so a blind capture of an hourly bug is hopeless. Trigger first, qualify second.
  • Storage qualification stretches the same buffer over ~100× more time on a bus that is idle 99 % of the time.
  • Set TRIGGER_POSITION mid-buffer so you capture the cause, not just the symptom.
  • One ILA per clock domain. Sampling a fast domain with a slow clock is an unsynchronized CDC that fabricates values. Cross-trigger between cores instead.
  • VIO outputs are asynchronous. Synchronize single bits with xpm_cdc_single, coherent fields with xpm_cdc_handshake.
  • Probe the state vector first. It finds more bugs than any data bus.
  • If the bug disappears when you add an ILA, you have learned it is timing or CDC marginality. Switch to report_timing_summary -check_timing_verbose and report_cdc.
  • Commands: create_debug_core, create_debug_port, connect_debug_port, set_property MARK_DEBUG, write_debug_probes, and CONTROL.CAPTURE_MODE / CONTROL.TRIGGER_POSITION in the hardware manager.
